name: Standard Route
beta: From the Maynard Burn (Tyler Peak) trailhead, a steep boot path climbs through rhododendron forest and past an old fire-break (the Maynard Burn track) to reach meadows and then the crest of Gray Wolf Ridge around 2.7 miles (~6,200 ft). Formal trail tread ends shortly after (~2.85 mi), and the final push to the summit is a cross-country scramble over a minor sub-summit and along the open ridge, arriving at Baldy's rocky, view-packed top at 3.6 miles. The route follows the Lower and Upper Maynard Burn Trail from the Maynard Burn (Tyler Peak) trailhead at the end of FR 2870-120, gaining a ridge crest via steep, sometimes faint tread through subalpine meadows and scree/talus to the Baldy summit block.
overview: Baldy's standard route is a steep trail hike/easy scramble on Gray Wolf Ridge in the northeastern Olympic Mountains, gaining Buckhorn Wilderness high ground before the final stretch crosses toward the Olympic National Park boundary near the summit. It follows the Lower and Upper Maynard Burn Trail (#816/#816.2) from the Dungeness River drainage, climbing a long switchbacking staircase through forest before breaking into open subalpine meadows and an easy ridge walk to a windswept, largely treeless summit. Class 1-2 on the standard line with no technical climbing; the ridge continuation toward Gray Wolf Mountain adds loose scree, exposure, and route-finding. Because it gains roughly 3,000 ft in about 2 miles, it's one of the steeper maintained-trail climbs in the Olympics.

current.approach: The climber/hiker trailhead is at the end of FR 2870 (signed Baldy/Tyler Peak trailhead, ~12-car gravel pullout, roughly 47.883, -123.143) in the Upper Dungeness drainage of the Hood Canal Ranger District. From the trailhead, follow the old roadbed a short distance; at about 0.3 mile the Baldy climber's path (Lower Maynard Burn Trail #816) splits off to the right and begins climbing in earnest. At roughly 0.5 mile (~3,600 ft) the trail crosses a decommissioned logging road. Mueller Creek parallels the route through these early switchbacks and is the last reliable water low on the mountain — top off here, especially in late summer. The only water higher up is a small meadow stream reached by a short, steep side path just below where the trail gains the ridge crest, and nothing flows above that. Around 1.3 miles the path crosses the old Maynard Burn track near a brief junction with the Upper Dungeness Trail (#833.2) before continuing up as the Upper Maynard Burn Trail (#816.2). Hikers describe this middle section as a relentless, eroded 'staircase' — expect a narrow tread (in spots barely a foot wide) sidehilling an eroding slope, crumbly footing crossing a rocky ravine, and faint, muddy tread through boggy meadow benches where flagging/cairns can be sparse. By about 2 miles the forest thins and Tyler Peak comes into view; by 2.7 miles (~6,200 ft) the trail gains the open ridge crest/saddle east of Baldy, with the first views north to the Strait of Juan de Fuca and Vancouver Island — this is also where the route leaves the trees for good, an important landmark for the return. From the saddle, a boot path continues west along the exposed ridge, over a false summit (roughly 6,500 ft, frequently mistaken for the true top and a common confusion point in poor visibility) to the actual summit at 3.6 miles / 6,808 ft, which has an old campsite. Total is about 7.2 miles and 3,800 ft round trip. The ridge is fully exposed to wind and cloud, and lingering snow can bury the boot path into June; carry a map/GPS track for the upper mountain.
approach_variant_names: Maynard Burn climbers' path from the Dungeness
current.descent: Descend the same Standard Route (out-and-back), and no rappelling is required (0 rappels) — this is a hike/scramble, not a technical rock route. The main descent hazard is route-finding: the boot path across the open ridge and meadow benches above ~6,200 ft is faint and easily lost in the fog/whiteout conditions that frequently roll in on this exposed summit, and several trip reports specifically describe hikers becoming disoriented near the false summit on the way down. Note landmarks on the way up — the false summit at roughly 6,500 ft, and the point at 2.7 miles/~6,200 ft where the trail first exits treeline onto the ridge — as handrails for the descent, and carry a GPS track of the ascent line if visibility is questionable. Once back below ~5,400 ft the route re-enters forest and the tread becomes obvious again, following the Upper Maynard Burn Trail (#816.2) down through the Lower Maynard Burn Trail (#816) switchbacks, crossing the old decommissioned road and Mueller Creek drainage, back to the FR 2870 trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rack needed - this is a hike/scramble with no roped climbing. No cams, nuts, or fixed anchors are used or needed by parties climbing the standard route.
current.pro_needs: None - no protection is placed on the standard route; it is unroped talus/scree hiking and scrambling. Rockfall/loose rock is the main hazard rather than a lack of protection quality, so party spacing and helmets matter more than rack size.
current.rope_note: No rope is carried on the standard route - it's an unroped Class 1-2 hike/scramble to a talus/scree summit with no rappels or exposed technical pitches. Not applicable.

name: East Face
beta: In October 1992 Peter Doorish's ascent of a route on the east face of Mount Baring, with Laura Woods, went at 5.10d, and he explicitly distinguished it from his other Baring-massif routes of that season by noting that all of them except the east face ascent were Grade V climbs of about fourteen pitches. That implies a shorter, lower-commitment line — probably Grade III or IV — but there is no recorded pitch count, no length, no topo and no description of the line itself. There is no evidence of a repeat ascent. Anyone going after it should treat it as an exploratory objective: identify the line from the ground, expect the same variable gneiss and vegetated ledges as the rest of the mountain, and be self-sufficient for retreat. The east side of Baring drops toward the upper Barclay Creek drainage and is not served by any climbers' path; the practical access is over or around the peak from the standard northwest-ridge approach, or up the east-side slopes from the Barclay Creek valley.
overview: A short, obscure 5.10d line on the east side of Mount Baring, climbed by Peter Doorish and Laura Woods in October 1992 as the last of Doorish's five new routes on the Baring massif that year. It is the only one of them that was not a Grade V, and it is essentially undocumented beyond a single first-ascent note.

current.approach: No approach is known for this route. The only fixed reference point is the Barclay Lake trailhead at about 2,280 ft, reached by turning north off US Highway 2 at milepost 42 in Baring onto Barclay Creek Road (FS Road 6024), crossing the railroad tracks, bearing left at the fork 0.2 miles up, and driving roughly 4.3-4.5 miles of gravel. From there, Barclay Creek Trail 1055 runs 2.2 miles up the valley to Barclay Lake beneath the north side. Reaching the east face requires either continuing up the Barclay Creek drainage past the lake and gaining the east-side slopes off-trail, or approaching over the mountain via the standard northwest-ridge climbers' path and traversing around. Neither is described, and a reconnaissance trip to identify the line and its base is strongly advised before committing to a climbing day.
current.descent: No descent is published for this route. If the line tops out on or near the summit ridge, the standard walk-off applies: from the summit take the base-jumper boot track down and west, swing counterclockwise across talus into the notch between the north and south summits at roughly 5,550-5,600 ft, descend the gully west into the boulder basin at about 4,900 ft, drop through heather and boulders onto the west/northwest ridge near 4,000 ft, and follow the steep, eroded climbers' path about 1,500 ft through old-growth forest to the abandoned logging road above the Barclay Lake trailhead — roughly three hours from the summit. If the route ends below the ridge, plan on rappelling your own line, which on a 1992 route with no recorded repeats means building every anchor yourself and carrying plenty of tat.
current.detailed_rack: No rack is published. For an exploratory 5.10d on Baring gneiss, carry a full traditional alpine rack: a set of nuts plus offsets, cams from tips to #3 with doubles in the finger-to-hand range, a few pitons and a hammer, 12-14 alpine draws and long slings, two ropes so you can rappel the line, a cordelette, and 20-30 feet of tat with a knife for leaving anchors.
current.pro_needs: Assume all protection is your own and that any fixed gear is from 1992 and unreliable. Plan for vegetated cracks that need cleaning, for stretches of poorly protected face climbing, and for the possibility that a pitch simply is not worth leading.

name: Northwest Ridge
beta: This line is also called the "South Scramble" (3rd class, Grade II) and the Northwest Ridge Route; they are the same line. From the Barclay Lake trailhead you do not follow the maintained lake trail — you take the abandoned logging road just uphill of it, find the cairned climbers' path at the first creek crossing, and go essentially straight up the forested west side. The path gains around 2,000 feet in about a mile to reach the ridge crest near 4,000 ft, follows the ridge east, drops below a cliff band, crosses a wooded gully and traverses into a boulder-filled basin at about 4,900 ft. From the basin, cross east and climb the obvious couloir/gully about 700 feet to the notch at roughly 5,550-5,600 ft between South Baring and the main peak. Turn north out of the notch, the angle eases, and easy class-3 scrambling on heather, talus and blocky gneiss leads a final quarter mile to the 6,127-ft north summit. Aim for the north summit — the south peak is lower and harder. The outing is rated Hard at 7.0 miles round trip with 3,500 ft of gain to a 6,129-ft high point; it is elsewhere described as closer to two miles one way with 3,700 ft of gain, or roughly 4,000 ft. The discrepancy is real and reflects different start points and how much of the logging-road walk is counted; either way the defining feature is gradient, not mileage.
overview: The standard route and the only non-technical way up Baring Mountain: a brutally steep climbers' boot path up the west/northwest side to a talus basin, then a gully to the notch between the north and south summits and an easy class-3 ridge scramble to the top. It is short in distance and enormous in gradient — roughly 3,500-4,000 feet of gain in about two to three and a half miles.

current.approach: Drive US Highway 2 to milepost 42 in Baring — the turnoff is directly across from Der Baring Store — and turn north onto Barclay Creek Road (Forest Service Road 6024). Cross the railroad tracks immediately, and about 0.2 miles up bear left at the fork. Follow the gravel road roughly 4.3-4.5 miles to the Barclay Lake trailhead at about 2,280 ft; there is parking for about 20 cars, a vault toilet and picnic tables, but no potable water. Do not start on Barclay Creek Trail 1055. Instead, walk about a third of a mile up the overgrown, abandoned logging road that continues uphill from the parking area, past the toilet. At the first creek crossing look right for a cairn marking the start of the climbers' path — you will cross the creek twice, which is a useful confirmation you are on the right track. From there the path climbs relentlessly and directly up the forested north/west side of the mountain, with pink flagging that may or may not be present, a short heavily eroded class-3 step where hand lines have been reported, and several places where the trail braids. Gain the ridge crest near 4,000 ft, follow it east for roughly a mile, then descend below the cliff bands on the south side, cross the wooded gully, and traverse up into the talus basin at about 4,900 ft. Navigation is straightforward from the basin onward.
approach_variant_names: Climbers' path behind the Barclay Lake trailhead outhouse
current.descent: Reverse the route exactly. Downclimb the easy class-3 ridge from the summit to the notch at roughly 5,550-5,600 ft, then descend the gully west into the boulder basin at about 4,900 ft — this is the crux of the descent when snow is present, since the headwall is steeper than it looks from above and a slip runs a long way. Face in and kick steps, or plunge-step carefully with an axe. From the basin, retrace the traverse below the cliff bands and back over the ridge, then commit to the long forested descent. That final 1,500-2,000 feet is the part that hurts: it is steep, eroded, root-and-mud, and slick when wet, with a short class-3 section that has had hand lines installed. Parties describe the descent gully as nasty when wet. Stay on the boot path; the temptation to cut straight down into the wrong drainage is the classic error on this mountain, and the forest slopes here are cliff-banded and have killed people. The path deposits you back on the abandoned logging road a third of a mile above the trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: No rock rack is needed. In snow season, some parties bring a short rope or 30m cord to belay or hand-line the steep snow headwall below the notch, and a picket if the party includes less experienced members. In dry season no technical gear is required.
current.pro_needs: None in the technical sense — there is no protectable rock climbing on this route. The only 'protection' decision is whether to rope or hand-line the steep snow headwall in the gully below the notch in spring conditions, which parties are reported doing.

name: North Face
beta: The route involves four major vertical steps. The lower approach consists of approximately 2,300 feet of brush fighting up steep cliffs through dense vegetation (slide alder, vine maple, devil's club). Establish Dolomite Camp at the base of the first step. The climbing involves vertical, delicate mixed terrain with roof sections requiring stirrup aid climbing on unusually hard rock (no specific rock type has been reliably sourced for this face) with poor natural protection. The crux is on the second step (400 feet) which features 120-degree roof sections and extremely delicate vertical climbing. On the lower brush sections, the first-ascent party fixed hundreds of feet of light ¼-inch rope hung from the brush to assist with load-hauling, with separate lengths of full-diameter climbing rope fixed at the most hazardous spots; double fixed ropes were placed specifically on the first step for hauling loads. Multiple attempts from 1951-1959 failed before the successful first ascent in 1960.
overview: Baring Mountain's North Face is one of the largest and most serious rock walls in the Cascades, rising roughly 3,000 feet above Barclay Lake. It is a committing, infrequently climbed alpine rock and mixed objective with significant loose rock and routefinding.

current.approach: Park at the Barclay Lake Trailhead (~2,280 ft, end of gravel Forest Road 6024/Barclay Creek Road off US-2 near the town of Baring); a Northwest Forest Pass is required at the self-issue kiosk. This is the same trailhead used for the Barclay Lake day-hike and for Baring's easier South/West Ridge route, but for the North Face, leave the signed Barclay Lake trail immediately — the climbers' boot path starts behind the outhouse rather than on the main trail. Follow an old, abandoned logging road for about 1/3 mile to a cairn (~2,450 ft) where a rough, unmaintained climbers' path splits off toward the base of the mountain — this is easy to miss and is not marked by any trail sign. From the cairn, the boot path climbs steep, loose dirt slopes and crosses the creek draining the face several times; stay close to the water to keep the correct line, since the tread is faint and frequently lost in the brush. At roughly 4,300 ft — about 2,000 ft of gain and 1.4 miles from the car — the path reaches Couloir Camp, the historic base camp used during the decade-long siege that produced the first ascent; it remains a reasonable first-night bivy for parties who want to break the approach into two shorter days. Above Couloir Camp, the route continues up between two precipitous, brush-and-cliff-covered rock ribs that flank a large couloir (snow often lingers here into August, so early-season parties may want an axe for this section) to reach the base of the North Face's first rock step at roughly 5,500 ft, about 1.8 miles from the trailhead. In total, the lower approach involves fighting through approximately 2,300 vertical feet of dense brush (slide alder, vine maple, devil's club) and forest before any technical rock climbing begins — expect around 7 hours from the trailhead to the base of the wall, and wear sturdy approach shoes or boots rather than carrying rock shoes for this section.
approach_variant_names: Barclay Lake trailhead to Couloir Camp and the North Face
current.descent: Do not plan to reverse the technical wall — virtually every account of climbing Baring's north face describes descending a separate walk-off line rather than rappelling the route from top to bottom. From the top of the wall, traverse west/climber's-left (some parties describe following an old 'base-jumper' boot path) around to a talus field and the notch between Baring's summits, then drop roughly 700 vertical feet through boulders and meadow to pick up a heather trail on skier's left. This connects to a game trail switchbacking down through old-growth forest, a roughly one-mile traverse along the ridgecrest, and then a steep switchbacking trail (~1,500 vertical ft) down to a clearing and old logging road that returns to the Barclay Lake Trailhead — about 3 hours car-to-summit-to-car for the descent leg on the routes this has been documented for. This walk-off is a scramble/hike, not a rappel descent, and no fixed rappel stations are established on it. That said, treat this as route- and finish-dependent: Baring's north face has multiple independent lines topping out at different points, some of which may not connect cleanly to the walk-off gully without downclimbing or short rope work, and the 1961 first-ascent party made long rappels down the upper walls to retreat/descend in fog when the walk-off wasn't known or reachable. If you retreat mid-route, or finish on a line that doesn't top out near the notch, be prepared to rappel — carry a 60m rope and rack for building anchors, since fixed/bolted rappel stations should not be assumed on this poorly-protected, historically loose-rock alpine wall; natural anchors (trees, horns, gear) are the norm. Given this uncertainty, treat rappel count as route-specific and unknown rather than fixed.
current.detailed_rack: No exact cam-by-cam list is documented for this specific route, so the rack below is a reasoned inference from route character: unusually hard rock (the first ascent recorded only that the rock is unusually hard, with piton cracks that all but vanish higher up — since 2013 it has been informally nicknamed Rhino Stone, but no mineral composition is recorded, so it should not be assumed to be granodiorite, rhyolite, or any other named rock type), a single ~5.10c crux headwall pitch, with the rest of the roughly 1000ft of technical climbing more moderate (5.6-5.9). A single alpine rack from small nuts through 3in cams, doubled in the 0.5-1.5in hand/finger range.
current.pro_needs: Comprehensive rack; the face is large and protection varies. Some old fixed pins on the route are unreliable — back them up rather than trust them.

name: North Buttress
beta: The most commonly climbed route on Bear Mountain's north face, established by Beckey and Fielding in 1967. The approach gains a glacier couloir on the west side of the north buttress. The upper buttress features seven roped pitches of excellent quality granitic rock with consistent protection. Route is usually climbed as a 2-3 day alpine adventure including a multi-day approach and descents.
overview: Bear Mountain's North Buttress is a serious, remote alpine rock route deep in North Cascades National Park near the Canadian border, first climbed by Fred Beckey and Mark Fielding in July 1967 (originally rated NCCS V, F8, A4; now typically climbed free around 5.10). It offers sustained, high-quality climbing up the steep, glaciated buttress in an extremely committing setting near the head of the Chilliwack/Bear Creek drainage. Note: unlike some older references claim, this route is not part of Steve Roper and Allen Steck's Fifty Classic Climbs of North America list.

current.approach: From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead (~3,100 ft, end of Ruth Creek Rd/FR-32) follow Hannegan Pass Trail #674 — nearly level for the first mile, then a steady grade — about 4 miles and 2,000 ft of gain to Hannegan Pass (5,100 ft), roughly 2.5-3 hours. Drop off the back (east) side of the pass and continue about 5 more miles, bearing right at the North Cascades National Park boundary onto the Chilliwack River Trail proper; this section loses elevation into the valley, passes U.S. Cabin backcountry camp, and reaches the Chilliwack River crossing (historically a hand-cable car — verify current status with the NPS, since a high-water ford here is a real hazard). Continue down-valley past Copper Creek/Brush Creek camps to the Bear Creek confluence, roughly 17 miles and 8-9 hours from the trailhead including the pass. At Bear Creek, leave the maintained trail: ford Bear Creek (can be a genuine, sketchy crossing during snowmelt) and climb steep, brushy timber eastward. Above treeline the brush turns to huckleberry and slide alder before opening into meadows above Ruta Lake; from there traverse the divide, skirting the south slopes of Points 6592 and 6822 and crossing a rock rib, to a broad saddle at about 6,480 ft — the standard high camp, with running water and heather tent sites. All told this is roughly 21 miles and about 6,500 ft of gain from the trailhead to camp, which most parties split over two days, camping on the Chilliwack River Trail near Brush Creek because the Bear Creek camp has been closed since the 2021 fire. A much shorter line (~9 miles to camp) starts from Chilliwack Lake Road in BC, but it crosses the border on foot where there is no port of entry and follows an overgrown, unmaintained tread after the first 1.7 miles; the Hannegan approach is the one to plan on. From high camp, the route itself begins with a descent: drop down steep scree trending climbers' right off the saddle, cross several minor gullies, and reach the toe of the small glacier/névé spilling from the couloir below the North Buttress (about 60-90 minutes); crampons and an axe are genuinely useful here even in summer. Climb the glacier/névé on the climber's-left side of the buttress and work into slabs leading to the corner system that marks the start of the technical climbing, staying alert for a moat where the névé meets rock.
approach_variant_names: Hannegan Pass and the Chilliwack River Trail to Bear Creek
From the Chilliwack Lake road on the Canadian side
current.descent: The standard descent off Bear Mountain's summit is a walk-off, not a rappel-mandatory line: traverse west/southwest staying on the south side of the summit crest, cross a notch/gap, and work across a snowfield that breaks the cliff bands above the Bear Creek drainage, then continue down easier 3rd-4th class terrain. A short, sometimes-loose 3rd class gully drops back down to the saddle camp at ~6,480 ft — about 1 hour and 1,400-1,500 ft of descent in good conditions. That said, this gully is exposed enough that a meaningful number of parties choose to back it up rather than down-climb it, especially with wet rock, a less-experienced partner, or an alpine-start-to-dusk timeline: a party that prefers not to downclimb it can rappel off natural anchors, though no rappel is required. There are no fixed bolted anchors on this remote, lightly-trafficked route — build natural anchors (horns, gear placements, slung blocks) and back up any old tat you find in place before weighting it. Below the gully, reverse the approach: regain the saddle, traverse back past Points 6822/6592 into the meadows above Ruta Lake, descend through brush and timber to re-ford Bear Creek, and rejoin the Chilliwack River Trail for the long hike back over Hannegan Pass to the trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: Single rack of cams from small (~0.4in) up to 3in max, doubled on the 0.5in, 0.75in, 1in, and 2in sizes — this specific doubling comes directly from a route-focused trip report and gear list, not a generic guess. Bring a set of stoppers/nuts for thinner, more delicate placements on the 5.6-5.10a pitches. No pitons needed on modern ascents (historic 1960s FA account mentions pins, but current parties climb it clean).
current.pro_needs: Protection is generally adequate on the upper buttress's crack systems across the 7 pitches (5.6-5.10a); doubled mid-size cams (0.5-2in) cover the bulk of placements, with the 5.10a section being the crux and best-protected pitch. The approach glacier couloir below the buttress crest is loose, unprotectable 4th-class snow/rock/debris terrain with rockfall exposure — no gear is placed there, move efficiently and avoid lingering below parties.
bivy: Meadow basin below the northwest-ridge saddle
current.rope_note: Descent from the North Buttress (Beckey/Fielding 1967 route, aka 'North Face Buttress') is reported as a 3rd/4th class scramble/walk back to camp — no technical rappels are known on the standard descent, so a single 60m rope is standard; doubles/half ropes are unnecessary unless bailing mid-route.

name: Church Lake Scramble
beta: From the Church Lake trailhead at the end of FS Road 3160, an easy but steep unofficial path climbs about 0.6 miles to Church Lake. From the lake the route continues around the shore and up through meadows toward a ridge/saddle above, then follows the ridge — which becomes steep but is 'nothing scary' — to a high point near peak 6066, with the final ~100 meters to the true summit requiring some class 3 scrambling on a narrow, occasionally exposed ridge. This is a hiker/scrambler route, not a roped climb; no technical gear is used on it.
overview: Bearpaw Mountain (6,091 ft) is a short, steep scramble summit above Church Lake, just east of Church Mountain in the Nooksack Ridge high country north of Mount Baker. It's reached by an unmaintained boot path (not an official Forest Service trail) from the end of FS Road 3160, off Canyon Creek Road, climbing past Church Lake and up open ridge/meadow terrain to a narrow, sometimes-exposed class 3 finish.

current.approach: From the FS 3160 road-end parking (roughly 48.957°N, 121.851°W, reached via Canyon Creek Road/FS 31 then FS 3160 as noted above), the route follows an unmaintained but well-worn boot path — not a numbered Forest Service trail, just a heavily used user track — that climbs steeply through forest for about 0.6-0.7 mile and roughly 400 ft of gain to Church Lake, a small emerald subalpine lake sitting in a cirque directly below Bearpaw's north side. This first pitch is the steepest sustained grade of the day. Skirt the lake along its east/left shore (best flat campsites are on the far side, useful if splitting the trip). Beyond the lake the trail fades into intermittent boot-path and cairns through meadows and heather benches; keep left (east) up the basin rim toward a broad knoll around 6,066 ft on the ridge separating Church Lake's basin from Bearpaw's summit block — this stretch accounts for most of the remaining ~900 ft of the route's 1,300 ft total gain over roughly 1.5 mi one-way (matching the ~5.9 km round trip). From the 6,066 ft knoll, drop slightly and traverse north across a rocky/heather bowl toward the base of Bearpaw's summit block; the final approximately 300 ft to the 6,091 ft summit is easy class 2-3 scrambling on generally solid rock and blocks, with mild exposure in the last pitch. Church Lake is the last reliable water source — carry water from there for the upper mountain. There is no maintained tread past the lake, so route-finding by cairns and boot-path is necessary, and in early/mid-season lingering snow on the steep initial slope above the lake and in the summit gullies can require an ice axe and caution; parties often find snow patches into July on shaded sections. In July the last four miles of the Forest Service road to the trailhead are steep and deeply rutted; a high-clearance all-wheel-drive or 4x4 vehicle is the safe choice, and a phone map may send you to a different trailhead, so aim for the road end.
approach_variant_names: FS-3160 road-end boot path to Church Lake, then the basin rim to the 6,066 ft knoll
current.descent: Descend the same line: from the summit, downclimb the class 2-3 scramble terrain back to the 6,066 ft knoll above Church Lake basin. From there most parties either retrace the rim/boot-path back down into the basin, or drop via a direct scree/dirt gully (chute) that cuts straight down from the ridge to the lake's shore, shortcutting the traverse — this chute is loose underfoot (scree and dirt over rock) and warrants care with footing and any parties below; if snow lingers in the chute (common into early summer) an ice axe and basic self-arrest awareness are worthwhile. From Church Lake, retrace the 0.6-0.7 mile boot path back down to the FS 3160 trailhead. This is a non-technical walk-off/downclimb scramble — no rope or rappelling is used on this route.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rock rack applies to this route. It is an unroped Class 2-3 scramble — no cams, nuts, rope, or protection are used at any point, including the final steep section below the summit.
current.pro_needs: None. This is an unroped scramble; there are no protectable technical moves. The final ~100m to the summit is loose Class 2-3 terrain handled by careful route-finding and hand-and-foot scrambling, not by placing gear.
current.rope_note: Mostly trail hiking to Church Lake, then steep off-trail path; only the final ~100m to the summit is scrambling. No rope used in any trip reports found.

name: Southwest Face
beta: From a camp near Dutch Miller Gap, ascend the left-hand of two parallel gullies on the SW Face (~1,000 ft, Class 3-4) to a ridge notch NW of the true summit, then climb the summit block in three short pitches (up to 5.6) to the top. Descend via three single-rope rappels and reverse the gully.
overview: A 3-pitch (up to 5.6) summit block sits atop roughly 1,000 ft of Class 3-4 gully scrambling on the SW Face; this is Bears Breast's original 1939 first-ascent line and its standard route, reached via a long approach to Dutch Miller Gap.

current.approach: From North Bend, take I-90 to exit 34, follow 468th Ave SE north 0.6 mi, then turn right onto Middle Fork Road (FS Road 56). Continue 12 miles (paved becoming rough) to where the road veers right, then drive ~5 more rough, high-clearance-recommended miles to the Dingford Creek Trailhead (~1,500 ft), where the road is gated and the Dutch Miller Gap Trail starts up the old roadbed. Hike the Middle Fork Snoqualmie on the Dutch Miller Gap Trail roughly 15 miles to Dutch Miller Gap, then continue to a camp below the SW Face. Total round-trip trail distance for the outing is about 30 miles, plus the scramble from camp to the summit and back.
approach_variant_names: Middle Fork Snoqualmie to Dutch Miller Gap, then a camp below the face
current.descent: From the summit, make three single-rope rappels (a single 50m rope is sufficient) down the west side of the summit block to the ridge notch, then downclimb the Class 3-4 gully system back to the base of the face. Route-finding through the ledges is the crux of the descent and is reported to be slower than the ascent (~4.7 hrs summit-to-camp vs. ~6.0 hrs camp-to-summit). Retrace the approach through Dutch Miller Gap and the Middle Fork trail back to the trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: One recorded ascent got by with ten stoppers plus two small cams and six runners for the whole route. A single 50m rope is enough for the rappels, but 60m or two 50m ropes let 3-person parties reach belay stances more comfortably.
current.pro_needs: Protection is minimal but adequate — small cams and stoppers protect the crack/dihedral pitch. The crux first pitch has marginal protection near an old, loose piton in broken rock; extra care is warranted there.

name: Berdeen Peak Scramble
beta: The only documented ascent (Abegg's party, Aug 2012) climbed directly over the peak's east side and NW slopes rather than contouring around a subsidiary spur, finding mostly Class 3 terrain that is 'steep and mossy' with one or two unavoidable Class 4 moves; careful selection of moss and rock holds was needed on loose ground. Reported Day 1 stats for the full push from the road (including the Porkbelly Ridge approach and a descent to camp beyond the summit) were +6,550 ft / -1,820 ft over 6.3 miles — most of that gain occurs on the way to Berdeen's summit, with the loss coming afterward on the descent toward camp, so treat the raw numbers as slightly inclusive of travel past the summit rather than a pure car-to-summit figure.
overview: Berdeen Peak rises above remote, turquoise Berdeen Lake in the Bacon Creek drainage of North Cascades National Park, about 1.25 miles east of 7,080-ft Hagan Mountain, within the NPS-designated 'Berdeen' cross-country zone. There is no trail: the peak is reached by a long, brushy off-trail approach from the end of Bacon Creek Road (Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie NF) near Marblemount, followed by a Class 3 (occasional low Class 4) scramble up the east ridge and NW slopes. It is seldom climbed as a standalone objective — most parties take it as the opening summit of longer Northern Pickets-area ridge traverses, such as the multi-day 'Mystery Ridge' enchainment (Berdeen-Hagan-Mystery-Pioneer-Crowder-Swiss-Whatcom-Easy-Mineral).

current.approach: From the end of Bacon Creek Road (~850 ft, Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie NF), an intermittent boot path continues briefly along the old roadbed and the east-bank benches of Bacon Creek before angling up onto Porkbelly Ridge, the broad forested spur that climbs northeast toward Berdeen Peak. There is no maintained, numbered trail here — this is an unofficial climbers'-path/bushwhack route — and tread comes and goes through slide alder, vine maple, and devil's club in the lower timber, easing somewhat in open forest and heather bands higher up. Porkbelly Ridge is one of the brushiest approach ridges in this part of the range, so treat the brush-fighting and route-finding through it as the day's real crux, not the scrambling above. Bacon Creek, crossed or paralleled within the first mile or so above the road-end, is the last easy, reliable water; above that, plan on carrying water or relying on occasional seeps/lingering snow patches until you're near Berdeen Lake. The ridge gains steadily and steeply — roughly 6,550 ft of cumulative gain and 6.3 miles are logged for the full push from the road-end, over Berdeen Peak, and down to a camp above Berdeen Lake. Higher up, the ridge passes from brush into subalpine parkland and then rock/heather benches below Berdeen Peak's east side. One line contours around the summit on a spur ridge to avoid the top entirely, but most parties instead climb directly over the 6,400–6,420 ft summit via the east ridge/east side: easy-to-moderate terrain, mostly low Class 3 with occasional short Class 4 moves on steep, mossy rock, where holds need to be chosen carefully since moss-covered rock is slick, especially wet. Loose blocks and exposed dirt/heather steps along the ridge crest are the main scramble-specific hazards; a helmet is worth carrying. Near the summit, Berdeen Lake's turquoise basin opens up to the north/northwest. North-facing terrain along the approach ridge can hold lingering snow well into midsummer.
current.descent: This is a scramble descent with no rappelling — walk/downclimb off, either back down the ascent line or via the peak's northwest slopes, which is how most parties link the summit to a camp above Berdeen Lake. From the top, descend the NW slopes on moderate Class 2–3 dirt, heather, and broken rock, losing roughly 500 ft to the basin above the lake, then rejoin the Porkbelly Ridge line to reverse the bushwhack back down through parkland and timber to Bacon Creek and the road-end trailhead. Stay on or near the ridge crest as long as practical on the way down — dropping off-ridge into the brushier side-drainages or the creek gully below adds substantial extra bushwhacking and is a common way to lose time. Loose, mossy rock immediately below the summit and steep brush lower on the ridge are the main hazards; because both the approach and the return are slow, brushy going, budget a genuinely full, strenuous day (or plan on the overnight camp above Berdeen Lake that most trip reports use) rather than treating this as a quick out-and-back. Parties continuing into a longer traverse (Hagan Mountain, Mystery Ridge, the Pickets) push on past Berdeen Lake instead of returning to the trailhead same-day.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rack is used on this route. The summit scramble is mostly Class 3 with one or two Class 4 moves on steep, mossy, loose rock; no rope or protection is reported placed or carried for it.
current.pro_needs: None needed — this is an unroped Class 3-4 scramble. The limiting factor is loose, mossy rock and careful hold selection, not a lack of protectable terrain, so gear is a non-issue; a helmet is the main protective item worth carrying given the reported rockfall/handhold-failure hazard.
bivy: Bacon Creek road end and Porkbelly Ridge
current.rope_note: No route-specific trip reports located for Berdeen Peak itself. Inferred from comparable Pasayten Class 3-4 scrambles (e.g. Big Craggy, Blackcap): standard scramble kit, ice axe for lingering snow, helmet for loose rock on Class 4 sections. No rope typically carried.

name: Dry Creek Route
beta: The most commonly climbed and most-described line to the summit, but every source treats it as a serious, committing objective rather than a straightforward scramble; no route on Big Four is easy. Parties have turned back after finding natural avalanche activity in the couloir, and describe the final downclimb as frightening even for experienced climbers.
overview: Big Four's standard/easiest line: a long, steep approach up the Dry Creek basin on the mountain's east side, followed by a steep couloir and an exposed traverse of red slabs onto the summit ridge, then along it to the true (higher, second) summit bump. There is no easy way up this peak -- even the 'standard' route involves sustained class 3-4 scrambling, a committing couloir, and a technical rappel/downclimb on the way out.

current.approach: From the Big Four Picnic Area / Ice Caves Trailhead (1,640 ft) on the Mountain Loop Highway, follow the paved nature-trail toward the ice caves, then leave the trail to cross the South Fork Stillaguamish River on a fallen log. Travel southeasterly through open forest roughly a mile to reach Dry Creek, then ascend through the lower basin -- in snow conditions via a hidden snow chute, in bare conditions via a series of class 3-4 ledges and ramps -- into the upper basin. From the upper basin, climb the steep main couloir, then traverse the exposed red slabs to gain the summit ridge.
approach_variant_names: South Fork log crossing to Dry Creek basin
current.descent: Most parties descend the same Dry Creek line they climbed. From the true summit, reverse the summit ridge over the lower (first) bump, then set up a roughly 60-meter rappel from a notch on the south ridge -- some parties have found a 60m rope barely reaches the anchor/chockstone. Below the rappel, bypass steep snow and waterfall-moistened rock to the side, then downclimb roughly two more rope-lengths of steep terrain to regain the lower basin before retracing the approach back across the South Fork Stillaguamish and out to the trailhead. In winter/spring, parties instead downclimb the Dry Creek couloir itself, which parties describe as a genuinely dangerous, insecure downclimb.
current.detailed_rack: A light rock rack plus a 60m rope for the descent rappel.
current.pro_needs: Protection is minimal and often not encountered until the descent rappel anchor; the route is more about steep, exposed scrambling/snow-climbing than sustained gear placements.

name: Northwest Ridge
beta: Big Four Mountain's first ascent came on July 19, 1931, when Forest Farr and Art Winder climbed the northwest ridge -- the original route to the summit. As with the mountain's other lines, this route begins from the Big Four viewpoint/ice caves trail approach on the Mountain Loop Highway.
overview: The historic original line to Big Four's summit, first climbed in 1931. Modern trip-report literature on Big Four is dominated by the Dry Creek, Tower, and Spindrift Couloir lines, so detailed contemporary route-finding notes for this specific ridge are sparse compared to those routes.

current.approach: Start at the Big Four Ice Caves trailhead on the Mountain Loop Highway (a Northwest Forest Pass is needed for parking). The Ice Caves trail is an easy, mostly boardwalk and paved path of about 1.1 miles each way with roughly 220 ft of gain, passing the old hotel site at the picnic area, crossing the South Fork Stillaguamish on a bridge, and opening into a meadow below the north side of the mountain. Leave the trail at the end and head across the open basin toward the foot of the north-side ridge you are climbing.
current.detailed_rack: Sustained class 3-4 scrambling on friable Swauk-Chuckanut sandstone/conglomerate calls for a light rack of nuts and small-to-mid cams plus slings for natural anchors — no bolted/fixed anchors are documented on this peak. A 60m rope covers the rappel typically needed on descent.
bivy: Big Four north-side staging and base bivouac

name: Spindrift Couloir
beta: First climbed March 2, 1996 by Bart Paull and Doug Littauer in a fast, ultralight, ~9-hour push with no bivy gear. The route starts up an 'ice ribbon' on the initial slabs (thin ice at roughly 65 degrees with a short 85-degree step), continues through the main couloir's three steps of mostly moderate terrain, and hits its crux about three-quarters height: a 100-foot pitch of nearly vertical ice, which gives way to steep, often runnelled snow. The upper section mixes rotten ice, shale, and drytooling moves up to roughly 95-degree angles before summit cornices, which may require tunneling through.
overview: A serious ice/mixed line up the central couloir system of Big Four's North Face, climbing névé and water ice through a bowl and headwall, with a near-vertical ice crux around three-quarters height, to mixed drytooling terrain and cornices just below the summit ridge.

current.approach: Walk the nearly wheelchair-accessible nature trail from the Big Four Picnic Area toward the Ice Caves, to the open basin below the North Face. From the trail's end, move right to find a break in the lower cliffs -- straightforward with adequate snow cover, but may require bushwhacking on the far right in sparse-snow years.
approach_variant_names: Ice Caves nature trail to the north face basin
current.descent: The route finishes on the summit ridge, well to the west of the true summit. Descent goes northwest, via rappels and steep downclimbing, to the col between Big Four and Hall Peak; from there, multiple tree-anchored rappels lead back down through the North Face bowl to the base of the face. Careful navigation is essential -- parties have mistakenly descended south instead of northwest in poor visibility.
current.detailed_rack: Full technical ice/mixed rack: ice screws, rock protection for the mixed upper section, v-threads or similar for rappel anchors, tree slings for the descent through the North Face bowl.
current.pro_needs: Protection on the upper mixed pitches is reported as marginal (rotten ice, shale); the crux ice pitch takes standard ice screw protection.
bivy: Big Four north-side staging and base bivouac

name: Going Down Under
beta: Starting from the Beckey-Tate approach, the route traverses sharply right over overlaps to a big ledge below an open-book corner. From there it climbs two classic, clean corner pitches — the second through a burly bulge at 5.11c, the route's crux — followed by a wide-crack section, then exits via easier cracks to the top of the wall.
overview: A five-pitch line on the south face sharing the Beckey-Tate approach before traversing right to two clean corner pitches, including a burly 5.11c bulge, then finishing up easier cracks to the top of the wall.

current.approach: Same south-face approach as Beckey-Tate: park at the Hairpin pullout on SR-20, follow the Kangaroo Temple/Wallaby Peak path along Early Winters Creek, cross the creek, and ascend the approach gully (left fork at the high Y-junction) to the base of the Beckey-Tate start, then traverse right across overlaps to the route's own start ledge.
approach_variant_names: The Hairpin pullout and the south-face gully to the Beckey-Tate base, then traverse right across the overlaps
current.descent: From the top of the route, join the standard descent: scramble to the notch just north of the true summit, then follow the loose scree-and-snow gully back down toward the Hairpin pullout, roughly two hours from the top.
current.detailed_rack: A rack similar to Beckey-Tate's — cams from small to #3-4 for the corner and crack systems, with attention to gear for the wide-crack section.
current.pro_needs: The corner pitches, including the 5.11c crux bulge, protect well with a standard trad rack; the traversing first pitch benefits from extra slings to manage rope drag.

name: Walkabout
beta: Climbed ground-up over three days, the route forces its way through vertical-to-overhanging, crackless monolithic granite low on the wall via aid climbing through multiple roof systems ('the Kangaroofs'), protected by seven bolts on the first three pitches with bolted anchors. Above the roofs the route continues on natural gear to the top. The FA team topped out at 2 a.m. on August 19, 2012, bivied on the summit, and descended the next morning via the Beckey-Tate line.
overview: A serious ground-up aid-and-free line up blank, overhanging roof systems nicknamed 'the Kangaroofs' low on the south face, established over three days in August 2012, with natural-gear free climbing above the bolted aid pitches.

current.approach: Same as Beckey-Tate/Kearney-Thomas: park at the Hairpin pullout on SR-20, follow the Kangaroo Temple/Wallaby Peak path south along Early Winters Creek, cross the creek, and ascend the prominent south-face approach gully (left fork at the high Y-junction). Expect 2.5-5 hours; water is unreliable late season.
current.descent: The first-ascent team bivied on the summit after topping out at 2 a.m. and descended the following morning via the Beckey-Tate line — scrambling to the notch just north of the summit, then following the loose scree-and-snow gully back toward the Hairpin pullout (roughly two hours from the summit).
current.detailed_rack: The first three pitches follow bolted anchors and seven protection bolts through blank, overhanging roof terrain ('the Kangaroofs') and require an aid rack (aiders/etriers, hooks as needed); above that the route goes on natural gear (a standard free-climbing cam/nut rack) to the summit.
current.pro_needs: Bolt-protected on the crux aid pitches low on the route; natural gear placements protect the free-climbing terrain above.

name: West Face / West Route
beta: This Grade II alpine route climbs about 200 feet of rock in three short pitches from the base of the summit block. The approach ascends parallel gullies on the west face of Kangaroo Ridge beneath Big Kangaroo. The route culminates in a steep, mostly unprotectable exposed 5.6 slab across the summit fin with a single rusty old bolt for protection.
overview: Big Kangaroo (8,326 ft) is the highest tower on Kangaroo Ridge, a jagged line of granite spires rising about two miles east of Washington Pass. This route — known as the West Face or West Route — is the original first-ascent line, climbed by Fred and Helmy Beckey with Walt Varney on June 21, 1942. It's a moderate Grade II outing: a steep gully approach up the west face followed by three short pitches of low-5th-class-to-5.6 climbing, finishing with an exposed, largely unprotected slab move to the small summit, guarded only by one old 1/4-inch bolt most parties don't trust.

current.approach: From the Hairpin Turn pullout on SR-20 (about 1 mile east of Washington Pass, near milepost 163), pick up the cairned climbers' trail on the west side of Early Winters Creek — the same start used for Kangaroo Temple and Wallaby Peak. Follow it roughly 0.5-0.7 mile through open timber to where it meets the edge of a talus/boulder field. Rather than continuing south toward Kangaroo Pass (the Kangaroo Temple line), leave the trail here and cross Early Winters Creek — normally an easy rock-hop, but treat it with respect during peak snowmelt or after rain, since there is no bridge. Once across, the route becomes an open boot-track/light bushwhack through slide alder and slabs, trending east into the basin below Big Kangaroo. Around 6,000 ft, aim for the broad, shallow west-facing gully that leads up toward the notch just north of the summit block, identifiable by a distinct chockstone partway up. The gully is loose underfoot (stay near its edges or on the thin vegetation for better footing rather than the center choss), and narrows with downsloping slabs about halfway — some parties bypass this by favoring the adjacent north-side gully. Rope up below the chockstone: the first of the route's three roped pitches passes it to the notch, the second traverses around the summit block, and the third climbs the summit slab. One-way gain to this point is roughly 2,700 ft over about 2 miles; budget 2.5-4 hours depending on snow and route-finding, longer early season when the gully still holds snow (carry a light axe/crampons through July). Total car-to-car time is commonly 6+ hours.
approach_variant_names: The Hairpin turnout, cross Early Winters Creek at the talus edge, then the west gully with the chockstone
current.descent: The route's final move is the crux of the whole outing: an exposed, essentially unprotected 5.6 slab move past a single old, rusty 1/4-inch bolt to the tiny summit. This is downclimbed or top-roped back to the belay stance rather than rappelled — there's no real anchor up top to rap from, and space on the summit is too small for a stance. From that belay/notch, two slung-block (tat) anchors serve the gully descent: the standard method is one single-rope rappel (a 60m rope is sufficient) using either anchor to get below the steepest, loosest section of the gully; some parties instead break this into two shorter rappels via an intermediate anchor lower down, particularly useful for retrieving gear cached near the chockstone. From the bottom of the rappel(s), downclimb/scree-surf the remaining gully back into the approach basin, re-cross Early Winters Creek, and pick up the climbers' trail back to the Hairpin Turn. Keep a helmet on for the whole descent — the gully sheds loose rock readily, especially with parties above or below.
current.detailed_rack: A single, light rack covers this 3-pitch, ~200ft route: a set of stoppers/nuts plus cams roughly 0.5 to 2 inches. Pitch 1 takes small gear to a sling belay; pitch 2 is mostly natural pro off a flake and a small block (sparse); pitch 3 (5.6) has a crack taking small cams about 20ft above the belay before the first piece.
current.pro_needs: Protection is thin in places, especially pitch 2, which several parties describe as sketchy with minimal anchoring options. The exposed summit move is essentially unprotectable 5.6 slab with only one old, rusty 1/4in bolt at the top — treat it as decorative, not a real anchor point. Rock quality is generally sound granite but the approach gullies below involve choss and bushwhacking.
bivy: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
Kangaroo Pass and the upper Early Winters Creek meadows
current.rope_note: One 60m rope is sufficient for the entire route. Descent is a single 60m rappel from two slung-block anchors at the notch (after a top-rope down-climb/up-climb shuffle past the summit using the old bolt as a directional only) — no double rope is needed.

name: West Ridge (Standard Route)
beta: From a roadside pullout on SR-20 east of Washington Pass, descend/cross Early Winters Creek and climb steeply up the Willow Creek drainage (brushy, staying on the north side) to about 5,000 ft where the grade eases. Continue up open basin terrain to roughly 7,000 ft, then cross a loose scree or snow slope (~400 ft) to gain the west ridge at a saddle near 7,400 ft. Follow the class 2 ridge crest to the base of the summit block, climb a short class 4/low-5th chimney/crack (about 50 ft) to a stance below the final slab, then make an unprotected 5.7-5.8 boulder move (often boosted via a shoulder stand) onto the roughly 20-ft summit friction slab and the true summit.
overview: The West Ridge is Big Snagtooth's standard route: a long, mostly non-technical off-trail approach and class 2 ridge walk that ends with two short, exposed technical steps — a class 4/low-5th chimney followed by an unprotectable 5.7-5.8 boulder/friction move — onto the small, airy true summit.

current.approach: Park in a highway pullout on SR-20 about 3.5 miles east of the Washington Pass summit (roughly 4,320 ft elevation). Descend to and cross Early Winters Creek, then head up into the Willow Creek valley, staying on the north side of the creek. The first ~3/4 mile up the valley is steep and can be very brushy in summer. Around 5,000 ft the slope eases; continue up loose/open terrain into the upper basin near 7,000 ft, then traverse a loose scree or snow slope for about 400 ft to reach the saddle on the west ridge (~7,400 ft). Stay left of the waterfall cliff band in the Willow Creek valley; angling right of the creek runs into cliffs. A higher log crossing a few hundred feet upstream of the lowest one keeps your feet drier on Early Winters Creek.
current.descent: From the summit, downclimb about 10 ft to a rappel anchor and rappel the short friction slab, then downclimb/scramble back to the top of the lower chimney and rappel (existing webbing/anchors reported) to the ridge below. From there, descend the class 2 west ridge back to the upper basin, retrace the scree/snow traverse, and descend the Willow Creek drainage (loose, brushy) back to the SR-20 pullout. A 30m rope is sufficient for both rappels. When afternoon snow turns punchy in May, descend the narrow gully east of your ascent gully rather than the one you climbed.
current.detailed_rack: A very light alpine rack is standard: 2 small cams and 2 medium cams cover the short protectable section below the final slab; a single 30m rope is enough for the two rappels off the summit block.
current.pro_needs: The crux 5.7-5.8 slab/boulder move on the true summit is essentially unprotectable and is often surmounted with a shoulder stand or boost rather than free-climbed on gear. The short class 4/low-5th chimney just below it is the only real placement opportunity and typically takes 2-3 small-to-medium cams.

name: East Ridge (Hardscrabble) Route
beta: From the gated trailhead, walk or bike the old Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road roughly 7 miles to the unmarked boot path for Hardscrabble Lakes (near the old Hardscrabble Horse Camp). Climb past lower and upper Hardscrabble Lakes, staying close to the inlet to avoid cliff bands on climber's left. From upper Hardscrabble Lake, climb a gully to a col, drop onto the open granite slab of the north slope, then follow the east ridge to the summit.
overview: The historically preferred line: approach past Hardscrabble Lakes to a col, drop onto open granite slabs on the north slope, then follow the east ridge to the summit. Considered easier route-finding than the Dingford/north-slope line, but now a much longer trip since the access road was gated at Dingford Creek.

current.approach: Start at the Dingford Creek Trailhead gate and walk (or mountain-bike) the closed Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road about 7 miles to the boot path for Hardscrabble Lakes, which starts roughly half a mile short of the old Hardscrabble Horse Camp, across the road from a large fallen log. Follow the climbers path east through forest to upper Hardscrabble Lake, staying near the inlet — straying left leads into cliff bands. The path from the old road to the lower lake is overgrown but cairned across the talus; fallen trees at each end of the talus make it easy to lose. Above the upper lake expect a brush bash to reach the talus gully, in both directions.
approach_variant_names: The gated Middle Fork road to the Hardscrabble Lakes boot path
current.descent: From the summit, retrace the east ridge onto the north-slope granite slab, climb back up to the col, and descend the gully to upper Hardscrabble Lake; follow the inlet-side climbers path back down to the lower lake and rejoin the old road for the multi-mile walk-out.
current.pro_needs: No technical protection is used; this is an unroped Class 2 scramble on trail, boot path, granite slab, and talus.
bivy: Hardscrabble Horse Camp, Middle Fork Snoqualmie

name: North Slope (Dingford) Route
beta: From the Dingford Creek Trailhead, follow the maintained Dingford Creek Trail past the Hester Lake Trail junction to Myrtle Lake, then leave the trail and work steep, brushy terrain up to Big Snow Lake. Traverse right around Snowflake Lake and ascend chutes/rock ribs onto the upper mountain's rock fields; the final approach to the summit is class 2-3 scrambling. Serious route-finding and bushwhacking are required, and failed attempts due to losing the line are common.
overview: The shorter and most commonly climbed line to the summit: an off-trail push from Myrtle Lake past Big Snow and Snowflake Lakes, up steep gullies/chutes to broad rock and snow slopes on the mountain's north side, finishing on class 2-3 terrain to the summit.

current.approach: Drive to the Dingford Creek Trailhead gate via Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Rd / FSR 56 (about 18 mi from North Bend; the last several miles are rough gravel, high-clearance recommended). Hike the Dingford Creek Trail roughly 3.2 mi to the Hester Lake Trail junction, continue left (east) toward Myrtle Lake (about 2 more miles). From Myrtle Lake, leave the trail and climb steep, increasingly brushy terrain toward Big Snow Lake, then traverse right around Snowflake Lake before ascending gullies/a snow couloir on the mountain's NW flank to the upper rock fields.
approach_variant_names: Dingford Creek Trail to Myrtle Lake, then off-trail past Big Snow and Snowflake Lakes
current.descent: Downclimb the same chutes/couloir used on ascent, taking care on crumbly, mossy rock and any residual snow or ice, especially early in the season; traverse back around Snowflake Lake, drop to Big Snow Lake, then pick a line down through brush to Myrtle Lake and follow the Dingford Creek Trail out to the trailhead.
current.pro_needs: Unroped scramble; no fixed protection used.

name: Northeast Ridge
beta: Considered a quintessential North Cascades ridge climb. From Wing Lake camp, snow slopes (following the hogsback moraine wide right, then traversing back left) lead to a notch/col between the Northeast Ridge and neighboring Point 8995. Above the col the ridge is a straightforward but sustained climb: mostly 3rd and 4th class with a low-5th-class crux (commonly rated 5.2-5.4, with some parties finding a short 5.5-ish move near the top) about halfway up, plus a scramble past several loose towers low on the ridge that are typically bypassed on ledges just off the crest. Rock quality is poor low on the route and improves noticeably higher up. Most parties simul-climb much of the terrain and rope up only for the low-5th sections. First ascended by Roger Jackson and Michael Kennedy on September 1, 1973.
overview: A sustained, position-rich ridge climb: moderate snow gains the ridge crest at a notch, which is then followed over several towers and along an airy crest through mostly 3rd/4th-class terrain with a low-5th-class crux roughly halfway to the summit.

current.approach: As for the South Ridge: Rainy Pass/Lake Ann trailhead on SR-20, via Heather Pass and Lewis Lake to a camp at Wing Lake (~6,900 ft). From camp, ascend snow (a small permanent snowfield/mini-glacier can persist below the col into September) toward the low point in the Northeast Ridge — following the hogsback moraine wide right and then traversing back left to the notch is reported to stay on more stable ground than a direct line. On fine early-October weekends, larch-season crowds fill the Rainy Pass lots and line the highway shoulder; start early to secure parking.
approach_variant_names: As for the South Ridge to Wing Lake, then the hogsback moraine wide right to the low point in the Northeast Ridge
current.descent: From the summit, work down and south toward the South Ridge route, using one rappel or a down-climb to get below the initial band of rock, then continuing south to the south col. From there the descent follows the South Ridge's loose, cairned gully (described by multiple parties as tedious and 'choss'-prone) back down to snow slopes and Wing Lake. Some parties glissade the snow lower down early in the season. In July parties leaving the south ridge either pick down steep dirt or take the snow; dirt to lower-angle snow, then a glissade, worked, and the scree beside the snow sheds rock.
current.detailed_rack: A light alpine rack is standard: a small set of cams (roughly 0.3-2 in) plus a handful of nuts, and a single skinny 60m rope — many parties simul-climb most of the 3rd/4th-class terrain and pitch out only the low-5th crux and any towers they choose not to bypass.
current.pro_needs: Protection is sparse and unreliable in the loose rock low on the ridge; gear placements improve on the better rock higher up. A rack biased toward small-to-medium cams and a few stoppers is sufficient — this is not a sustained crack climb, and running belays/simul-climbing are the norm.
bivy: Rainy Pass trailhead lots, and the quarter-mile camping closures

name: Black Systems Solar
beta: Two-pitch sport climb on a lower west-facing wall section of Keechelus Ridge. Can be climbed as one continuous pitch or split into two pitches using mid-route anchors. Described as one of the best 5.9s in Washington with commanding views from the belay stations. Belay ledge provides excellent sun protection during morning and midday hours.
overview: 5.9 sport route on Keechelus Ridge, featuring accessible climbing with excellent views and described as one of the best 5.9s in Washington.

current.approach: From Seattle, drive east on I-90 to Snoqualmie Pass and take Exit 54, crossing to the north side of the freeway before turning onto FR 4832, then following it onto FR 4934 to the small trailhead pullout. On foot, cross the road and hike up a spur road for about 15 minutes to a flat bench, then pick up a cairned trail heading north into the forest to a rocky area, staying on the main climber's trail through a short, steeper forest section to reach the crag — roughly 25-30 minutes total from the car. A Northwest Forest Pass is generally expected for parking at national forest trailheads in this corridor.
current.descent: A 70m rope will not reach the ground when lowering from the top anchors — descend via the mid-height anchor in two stages, or simply lower each pitch in turn if climbing it as two pitches.
current.detailed_rack: 17 bolts with 2 chain anchors. Alpine draws recommended.
current.pro_needs: Sport climbing with full bolt protection. Mid-route anchors allow for two-pitch option.
current.rope_note: 2-pitch bolted sport route (130 ft/39m total), 17 bolts, 2 chain anchors mid-route. A 70m rope is NOT enough to lower from the upper anchor in one go — either climb/rap in two pitches using the mid anchors, or alpine-sling the lower bolts and back-clean on a single continuous lead.

name: Standard Scramble
beta: Multiple independently-published trip reports (2006, 2013, 2023, and a winter ski ascent) describe the same standard line: gain the northeast ridge either from the Eureka Creek drainage to the north or from a col below the peak reached via Shellrock Basin/Shellrock Pass to the south, then follow class 2-3 talus, scree, and blocky black-hornfels terrain along the ridge crest to the summit. Sources explicitly note the route can be done without a rope, including in winter snow conditions. It is almost always climbed as part of a multi-day traverse with neighboring Mt. Lago, Mt. Carru, and/or Osceola Peak, since all share the same Shellrock Basin approach.
overview: Blackcap Mountain (8,402 ft, surveyed by differential GPS; older USGS quads list 8,397 ft) is a remote summit in the northern Pasayten Wilderness, part of the Monument-Lago-Carru-Osceola-Lost Peak cluster near the WA/BC border. Its dark summit block of black hornfels/shale — visibly distinct from the lighter rock below — gives the peak its name. With only 406 ft of prominence it just qualifies for Washington's Top 100 (Bulger) list, and it is almost always climbed as one leg of a multi-day traverse of the surrounding Top-100 summits (commonly Osceola-Carru-Lago-Blackcap-Lost) rather than as a stand-alone objective, since the nearest trailheads are 15+ miles away.

current.approach: Blackcap sits deep in the Pasayten Wilderness and is reached almost entirely off-trail after a long, multi-day trail approach — there is no short car-to-summit option. The standard approach starts at the Buckskin Ridge Trailhead at Slate Pass (~6,900 ft) on Slate Peak Road, the spur above Harts Pass off FS-5400 and the highest trailhead in Washington reached by road. From the trailhead, follow the Buckskin Ridge Trail over Slate Pass for about 0.9 mile, then take the Whistler Cutoff down into the Middle Fork Pasayten valley to Robinson Creek/Middle Fork Pasayten Trail #478, about 4 miles in. Follow the Middle Fork downstream (north) for about five miles, then climb to Fred's Lake, a reliable water source and the usual first-night camp (about 5 hours trailhead-to-camp at a backpacking pace). A longer alternative starts low at the Robinson Creek Trailhead on the Lost River Road and crosses Robinson Pass into the same valley. Day two, climb from Fred's Lake to 7,100-ft Rolo Pass on the ridge crest above the lake; Lake Doris is a short side trip from here. From Rolo Pass, drop into Upper Eureka Creek (another dependable water source) and cross east into scenic Shellrock Basin, then climb to 7,500-ft Shellrock Pass — a full trail day of roughly 2.5-3 hours from Fred's Lake. Camp is typically made in Shellrock Basin, just below and east of the pass. From camp, leave the trail at Shellrock Pass and traverse SSW across an open, grassy/rocky basin, staying below the cliff bands, to the base of a talus slope; work the left (east) edge of the talus south to a saddle/col just west of the cliff terminus, directly below Blackcap's east face — this off-trail link is about 1-1.5 miles and 1,000-1,500 ft of gain/loss with real route-finding (a steep snowfield below Shellrock Pass often needs to be bypassed on the left in early season — carry an axe if snow persists). From the col, scramble up loose scree and talus on Blackcap's east face to gain the northeast ridge, where the rock transitions to distinctive black hornfels/shale; follow the ridge (staying on its left/south side as terrain allows) on easy Class 2-3 with some exposure and loose rock near the top to the summit. Camp-to-summit is about 5-6 hours round trip. An alternate eastern approach exists via the Monument Creek Trail, leaving it a few miles before Butte Pass where Monument Creek bends west into the open Monument-Blackcap basin, then climbing that basin's cliff band on either flank to reach the same upper mountain — but the Shellrock Pass approach described above is the standard, most-traveled line. Either way this is a serious wilderness undertaking: expect 30-35+ round-trip miles and 3-5 days car-to-car, with the Middle Fork Pasayten River crossing running high and cold in early season and long stretches of trail that can be brushy or storm-damaged in a given year.
approach_variant_names: Shellrock Basin camp and the traverse to the east-face col
Robinson Creek over Robinson Pass
Monument Creek and the Monument-Blackcap basin
current.descent: This is a scramble with no rappelling — descend by reversing the ascent line. From the black-hornfels summit, downclimb the northeast ridge (Class 2-3, loose in spots) back down to the east-face scree/talus, which is noticeably looser and more hazardous descending than ascending — plan on a slow, controlled downclimb with attention to kicking rock onto anyone below. Continue down the scree/talus to the col, then reverse the off-trail traverse (talus edge, then NNE across the grassy/rocky basin) back over to Shellrock Pass, re-bypassing the snowfield if it was present on the way in, and drop back to camp in Shellrock Basin. From there the return to the trailhead simply reverses the multi-day trail approach: Shellrock Basin to Shellrock Pass, over Rolo Pass, past Fred's Lake, down to and along the Middle Fork Pasayten River, back up the Whistler Cutoff and over Slate Pass, and out to the Buckskin Ridge Trailhead. No technical gear (rope, rack, harness) is needed anywhere on this route; a helmet and trekking poles/ice axe (for any lingering snow near Shellrock Pass) are the only extras worth carrying. This is a full walk-off/downclimb.
current.detailed_rack: None needed — the standard route is a non-technical class 2-3 scramble; trip reports (including a winter ascent) note the party carried no rope.
current.pro_needs: No protection is placed on this route. It is an unroped Class 2-3 scramble: talus and scree up to the ridge, then a class 2 ridge walk with one or two class 3 moves through loose rock near the summit's distinctive black hornfels cap. Rock quality on the cap itself is described as solid but the approach slopes/gullies are loose — a helmet is the main protective item recommended, not a rack. No trip report reviewed (from either the NE-ridge/Shellrock Pass side or the east Monument Creek basin side) mentions placing gear.
bivy: Doris Lake and Freds Lake basins
Shellrock Pass, Shellrock Basin and the Eureka Creek meadows
current.rope_note: East Ridge from the saddle is mostly Class 2 with one or two Class 3 moves and some exposure on loose rock near the 'black cap' summit block. Ice axe advisable in early season; no rope/rack needed from Shellrock Pass approach.

name: Bleed for the Chodecophagus
beta: Extends the Sarcophagus line up the obvious straight-up headwall after the orange streak in the middle of the wall. Stand on the ledge boulder, clip two draws high, then start crimping through sustained climbing; holds improve near the final bolt. Two tactical options exist: carefully skip/back-clean certain bolts per a detailed clipping strategy to reduce rope drag, or take a ledge traverse and climb the extension directly off the ledge.
overview: The wall's hardest route — a sustained, straight-up headwall extension of the line taken by Crescendo of the Sarcophagus Breathing.

current.approach: Same base area as Crescendo of the Sarcophagus Breathing; the route climbs the headwall extension above/right of it.
current.descent: A full 70-meter rope is required to lower from the anchor given the route's length.
current.detailed_rack: Fully bolted, approximately 15-16 bolts; requires careful clipping/back-cleaning sequencing to manage rope drag over its length.
current.pro_needs: Sport rack of 15-16 quickdraws; plan the clipping sequence in advance to avoid rope drag on this long, sustained pitch.

name: Blood Sport
beta: Steep start off a left-hand side-pull, placing a #1 Camalot into a pod before clipping into bolted protection; a rest ledge partway up breaks the pitch before a pumpy, sustained bolted sequence moving left and up to the anchor.
overview: A 50ft single-pitch sport/mixed route on Guye Peak in the Snoqualmie Pass area, combining bolt protection with one traditional gear placement; ends at a 2-bolt chain anchor with no top-out.

current.approach: From I-90 Exit 52, follow Alpental Road up to the ski area and park at the Alpental ski-area lot (the Snow Lake trailhead parking) or in a legal spot along Alpental Road itself. The side roads named 'Strasse' are private, and since 2021 residents have barred climbers from driving or walking on them. For the south-face/rock routes, the crag rises directly above the parking area with essentially no approach hike required. For routes on other aspects of the mountain, use the Commonwealth Basin/PCT North Trailhead a short distance up the highway instead, following the Pacific Crest Trail into Commonwealth Basin before cutting up toward the peak. Because of the short, direct access, Guye Peak is climbed both summer and winter, though rock routes are primarily a snow-free-season (summer-fall) objective.
approach_variant_names: Alpental lot, boot path east along the base of the South Rib
current.descent: Lower directly from the fixed 2-bolt chain anchor at the top of the pitch; no rappel or walk-off required.
current.detailed_rack: A rack of quickdraws for the bolted sections plus one #1 Camalot for a pod near the start; fixed 2-bolt chain anchor at the top.
current.pro_needs: Mostly bolt-protected; carry a single #1 Camalot for the pod low on the route in addition to quickdraws.
current.rope_note: Guye Peak, 5.11b, 50ft sport/mixed pitch - bolts plus one #1 Camalot placement into a pod near the start; 2-bolt chain anchor, no top-out.

name: Cascadian Route
beta: First ascended by Eric Wehrly and Sam Boyce in August 2023. Grade V, 5.10+, 16 pitches, with just over 2,000 ft of net elevation gain and about 2,800 ft of total climbing distance on the west face of the Southwest Summit (9,320'). The route sits 'looker's right' of its established neighbors, the Soviet and Oregonian routes. A weathered, decades-old cam found at pitch 4 suggests a prior abandoned attempt on similar terrain.
overview: A modern (2023) 16-pitch, V 5.10+ line up the west face of Bonanza's Southwest Summit, established to the right of the older Soviet and Oregonian routes on the same wall.

current.approach: Multi-stage approach (~11+ miles): drive to Chelan, ferry to Lucerne, bus to Holden Village, then hike to a camp at about 7,000 ft near the North Star-Bonanza col - a full day of travel and approach.
approach_variant_names: The North Star-Bonanza col, then talus south to the white slabs beside the caret-shaped snowpatch
current.descent: From the Southwest Summit, downclimb/traverse to the Isella Glacier and descend along an undulating line of steep rock and moraine at about two-thirds of the glacier's height, then cross through a notch in the south ridge to regain the North Star-Bonanza col camp.
current.detailed_rack: A rack suited to sustained 5.10+ trad climbing on loose rock; extra small-to-medium cams recommended given the choss and run-out sections.
current.pro_needs: Protection is often difficult on the loose, run-out pitches, especially 11-12; a careful, well-stocked rack is advised.

name: Mary Green Glacier (Standard Route)
beta: From Holden basecamp (Holden Lake or Holden Pass), approach via established trail to glacier base at ~7,300 ft. Rope up and ascend Mary Green Glacier bearing west along its north edge, then traverse southwest to the glacier's upper corner. Climb the steep upper snow finger to the right until reaching rock; transition to the northeast ridge with mostly Class 3-4 rock just right of a gully for several rope lengths, then traverse left to a prominent notch in the upper ridge north of summit. Scramble Class 4 loose ridge crest past large blocks to the summit horn.
overview: Bonanza Peak (9,511 ft) is the highest non-volcanic summit in Washington and the highpoint of Chelan County. The Mary Green Glacier route — first climbed in 1937 by Curtis Ijames, Barrie James, and Joe Leuthold (Mazamas) — is the peak's classic standard line, ascending its eastern side. Reached only via the Lady of the Lake ferry up Lake Chelan and the remote trail-and-boat village of Holden, the climb combines glacier travel and a moat crossing with a short, exposed Class 3-4 rock finish to a summit deep in the Glacier Peak Wilderness. From the Holden Campground trailhead it's roughly 14 miles round trip with about 6,300 ft of elevation gain to the summit, on top of the multi-day boat-and-trail approach just to reach that trailhead.

current.approach: From Holden Village (~3,300') walk the gravel road/Railroad Creek Trail (FST 1256) west about 0.9 mile to the signed junction with the Holden Lake Trail and bear right (north). The Holden Lake Trail climbs steadily for about 4 miles through forest, brush, and a few small side-creek crossings (reliable water) to Holden Lake (5,278'), set in a cirque directly below Bonanza's east face — a natural camp and last easy water before things get rougher. From the lake's outlet the tread becomes increasingly faint, skirting the north shore through slide alder and talus (real bushwhacking and route-finding here, especially early season with high water), then climbing a hillside traverse northwest to Holden Pass (6,360'), the standard high camp and last reliable water before committing to the glacier. From the pass, make a rising traverse west along the ridge/slope to a snowfield beneath rock slabs around 7,000–7,300'; scramble the class 3 slabs — start high and right to skirt a waterfall — to gain the northern edge of the Mary Green Glacier. All told, roughly 5 miles and ~3,000' gain from Holden Village to high camp, then another ~3,000' of glacier and summit rock above that. Hazards: black flies between 3,000–4,000' and mosquitoes from the lake upward; loose, rockfall-prone gullies below the glacier's retreating margin (stay left/out of the fall line where other parties may be above); and a moat crossing near the top that is usually just a short step across onto rock. From the glacier's northern edge, ascend bearing west along its north (climber's right) edge, then traverse southwest along the base of Bonanza's NE ridge to the glacier's upper corner before crossing the moat.
approach_variant_names: Holden Village via the Lake Chelan ferry, then Holden Lake and Holden Pass
current.descent: Reverse the route: down-climb the summit ridge and rocky rib back toward the glacier, staying climber's left of the standard line to dodge rockfall funneling down the gullies. The established descent uses 6–7 fixed rappel stations (horns, flakes, and slung boulders left by prior parties) along the class 3–4 rock band, typically consolidated into about four rappels using a 60m x 8mm rope — a common sequence is one rappel off the east ridge into the upper gully, then three more down through the rock to within roughly 200 feet of the glacier, where you downclimb or walk the rest onto snow. One frequently-used anchor sits on a large boulder/flake at a wet slab lower on the route; multiple trip reports flag it as sketchy and overdue for fresh webbing, so back it up or extend it rather than trusting it outright.
