Inspect every fixed station before weighting it — Cascades alpine anchors get sun-bleached, chewed by rockfall, or buried season to season. Parties comfortable downclimbing exposed 3rd/easy 4th class can skip some of the raps. Once back on the glacier, recross the moat and descend to Holden Pass camp.
current.detailed_rack: Minimal to no rock rack — most parties carry no cams/nuts at all for the Class 3-4 (up to low-5th, 5.0-5.6) rock above the glacier; many parties leave the rock rack at home. What's actually used is a handful of slings (including a couple of double-length 120cm runners) for building anchors around blocks/horns on the summit scramble and for the rappel stations on the loose-rock/waterfall-slab descent gully — one party notes a long (triple-length) sling is worth replacing a worn one at the wet-slab rappel station.
current.pro_needs: Protection is essentially non-existent on the upper mountain — the Class 3-4 ridge/gully climbing to the summit is typically soloed or simul-climbed by experienced parties rather than protected with placed gear. The real protection need is glacier travel gear (roped travel, pickets for crevasse crossings) and reliable natural rappel anchors (slung horns/blocks) for the loose descent.
current.rope_note: Standard route: glacier travel to steep upper snow finger, then Class 3-4 rock for several rope-lengths to a notch below the summit. Reported setups vary: 2x40m ropes (one for glacier travel, both combined for rappels), a 70m rope, or a single 50-60m rope; skilled parties often downclimb the rock unroped but rappel the descent. Crevasse hazard is real even when the rock is soloed.

name: Northeast Buttress
beta: From the buttress base (~8,350 ft), the ridge steepens and narrows quickly. Climbing is mostly solid rock but lichen-covered in places, with sustained sections in the 5.7 range and sections of wild exposure along the crest. Expect roughly 4 hours of climbing from the buttress base to Bonanza's true (main) summit.
overview: Bonanza Peak is the highest non-volcanic summit in Washington. This route is the Northeast Buttress, a serious, mostly-rock alpine line that gains Bonanza's true (9,516') summit directly, branching off the standard Mary Green Glacier approach at about 8,350 ft. Climbing in the 5.7 range (the V, 5.7/5.8 grade belongs to the full three-summit traverse it begins), the Northeast Buttress offers sustained, exposed ridge climbing on generally solid but lichen-covered rock, deep in the Glacier Peak Wilderness above Holden and Lake Chelan.

current.approach: The approach follows the same trailhead-in as the standard route — Railroad Creek Trail (FST 1256) from Holden Village to the Holden Lake Trail junction, then up to Holden Lake (5,278') and Holden Pass (6,360') for high camp — but instead of angling onto the Mary Green Glacier itself, continue on benches and talus/heather to climber's right (east/north side) of the glacier. This adds roughly another 3 hours and substantial elevation gain beyond Holden Pass to reach the base of the Northeast Buttress/Face around 8,350'. Total gain ends up close to the standard Mary Green line's, since both leave the same camp and finish on the same summit. Water sources match the standard approach (Holden Lake, Holden Pass); above the pass, plan on carrying what you need since there's little reliable water on the buttress approach itself. Expect loose rock and routefinding on the benches, and — because this line stays right of the glacier on rock rather than crossing snow/ice — less exposure to crevasse hazard but more exposure to rockfall and unconsolidated talus underfoot. Past Holden Lake the path can vanish into avalanche debris in early July; keeping to the right-hand (north) trail on the way to the pass avoids a swampy wade.
approach_variant_names: Holden Village to Holden Lake and Holden Pass, then the Mary Green's north margin to the buttress toe
current.descent: The straightforward descent reverses down to the Mary Green Glacier and follows the standard route's descent: down-climb the summit ridge/rock rib, use the fixed rappel stations through the class 3–4 band (about four rappels with a 60m rope, 8mm lines are common), cross the moat, and descend the glacier to Holden Pass camp — see the Mary Green Glacier route's descent notes for full detail on that shared lower section. Parties combining this face with a full three-summit traverse instead descend from the Southwest Peak via ledges onto the Isella Glacier's upper snowfields, traverse to the Southeast (Holden) Ridge, climb a short ~5.7 chimney, and then make a single rappel from the col back down onto the Mary Green Glacier before rejoining the standard glacier descent to camp. Either way, expect loose rock on the upper buttress and ridge sections and take care with rope management around the gendarmes and notches. On the way down in July, the waterfall slabs below the glacier are slippery wherever wet and some steps have piton anchors for a short rappel; belaying across the moat at the glacier edge is common.
current.detailed_rack: A single set of nuts and cams from finger-size to about 2-3in covers the 5.7/5.8 climbing — steep, narrow terrain right off the toe of the buttress, then simul-climbable ridge crest with at least one full 60m pitch through a chimney partway up. Doubling up thin-to-hand cams (roughly 0.4-1in) is a reasonable add given long simul-climbed stretches with sparse pro on a wandering ridge line, but no exact size-by-size list is known.
current.pro_needs: The steep lower buttress and the chimney pitch take gear well, but the long ridge-crest sections above are described as exposed and were largely simul-climbed rather than pitched out — expect runout stretches
bivy: Holden Pass and the slab bivies above

name: Oregonian Route
beta: First ascended by Seth Keena and Erik Bonnett in early September 2013 (ascent dated 9/4/2013). Rated V, 5.9+, 2,200 ft total: 1,600 ft of new terrain (mostly sustained 5.6-5.8 with moves to 5.9+, via ramp/ledge systems) then 600 ft shared with the Soviet Route to the summit. It begins a few hundred yards left of the Soviet Route, making the Soviet and Oregonian the two established lines on this northwest wall. The first-ascent team's approach that year was an unusually long ~32-mile one-way trip (including ~10 miles of biking) due to ferry/road closures in effect at the time - this is not the standard approach.
overview: A V 5.9+ line on the northwest buttress of Bonanza's Southwest Peak that climbs 1,600 ft of independent terrain before joining the Soviet Route for its final 600 ft to the summit block.

current.approach: Standard approach follows the same Lucerne ferry -> Holden Village -> hike to the North Star-Bonanza col camp used for the Soviet Route; the first-ascent party's much longer bike-and-hike approach was due to temporary ferry/road closures in 2013 and is not typical.
approach_variant_names: The North Star-Bonanza col, then past the Soviet buttress and across the pocket glacier
current.descent: The route ends on the southwest summit (about 9,320 ft) after merging with the upper Soviet Route, and the way down is the same as for that route. Follow the crest northeast to the West Peak, which takes close to two hours because the gendarmes are mostly bypassed on third and fourth class ledges with one short rappel. From the West Peak, downclimb talus on the northwest side to a band of steep slabs, then make two rappels of about 200 ft each; anchors are improvised from natural features, so carry cord and a few nuts or pitons. Below the slabs, downclimb to the talus, traverse beneath the buttress to the North Star-Bonanza col, and expect to arrive at camp very late after a full day. The steep south face descent over glaciers and cliffs is the alternative, but it is long and committing.
current.detailed_rack: A rack for sustained 5.6-5.9+ trad climbing typical of North Cascades alpine rock, per the route's ramp/ledge character.
current.pro_needs: No detailed pitch-by-pitch protection beta was found; expect trad protection throughout the sustained 5.6-5.9+ climbing.

name: Northeast Face
beta: From a camp near the head of Park Creek, climb easier cliffs to a small glacier at the base of the face, then go left up the glacier to an icefall and traverse right through and under it (reported as a genuinely exposed, 'frightening' crossing) to reach the main rock wall. Follow a prominent central rib essentially straight up the face on generally sound Cascade granodiorite/orthogneiss, through a crumbly red rock stratum that crosses the whole face at roughly mid-height, to a 100-foot notch near the summit, then on to the top. The face averages about 70 degrees and is over 3,000 feet high.
overview: A rarely-repeated alpine rock route up the prominent central rib of Booker's 3,000+ foot Northeast Face, one of the steepest walls in Washington, first climbed via an icefall approach and a crumbly mid-face rock band to a notch just below the summit.

current.approach: Approach via a multi-day backpack toward Park Creek Pass/the head of Park Creek (from the Thunder Creek Trail out of Colonial Creek Campground, or as part of a Buckner-area traverse), then camp near the base of the face for an alpine start.
approach_variant_names: Head of Park Creek: easier cliffs to the small glacier, then right through the icefall
Park Creek trail from the Stehekin valley
current.descent: From the summit, descend the ordinary route down to the Booker-Buckner col and back toward a Park Creek-area camp — the same descent used by the first-ascent party, who found their camp again just before dark.
current.detailed_rack: A light alpine rock rack (set of nuts, cams to roughly 3 inches) for the class 4-5 rib; consider pickets/screws for the approach glacier and icefall traverse.
current.pro_needs: Standard trad protection for the class 4-5 rib climbing; extra care placing protection in the crumbly red stratum band at mid-height, which the first-ascent party specifically noted as looser than the otherwise sound surrounding rock.
bivy: Five Mile Camp, Park Creek trail

name: Northwest Route
beta: From a camp at or near Park Creek Pass, ascend toward the Booker-Buckner col, crossing a broad sandy gully around 6,900 ft roughly a mile from the pass; a few crevasses/cracks near the col are typically bypassed on snowbridges. From the col, the northwest side of Booker is mostly Class 3 scrambling with some easy Class 2-3 terrain to the summit.
overview: An alternate Class 3 scramble reached from Park Creek Pass via the Booker-Buckner col, on the mountain's northwest side; used mainly by parties already in the Park Creek/Buckner area on a multi-day traverse rather than as a dedicated approach.

current.approach: Reached via a multi-day backpack up the Thunder Creek Trail from Colonial Creek Campground to Park Creek Pass (roughly 40 miles round trip with on the order of 7,000 ft of cumulative gain including the bonus climb to Junction Camp), or as part of a Ptarmigan-style traverse linking Cascade Pass/Buckner/Park Creek Pass. From a Park Creek Pass-area camp, it is a short day-trip scramble up to the Booker-Buckner col and on to the summit.
approach_variant_names: Park Creek Pass, the sandy gully and the rocky point, then up to the Booker-Buckner col
current.descent: Downclimb the northwest-side Class 3 terrain back to the Booker-Buckner col, then descend the broad sandy gully (using snowbridges over any crevasses/cracks as on the ascent) back toward Park Creek Pass camp.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rack needed; this is an unroped scramble aside from the snow/glacier travel gear used to cross the col.
bivy: Five Mile Camp, Park Creek trail

name: South Ridge
beta: Most parties combine Booker with Buckner Mountain in the same trip since both share the Cascade Pass/Sahale Arm approach and the Horseshoe Basin traverse. From Sahale Camp/Sahale Arm, descend Sahale's south side to a snow-free gully near 6,600 ft into Horseshoe Basin, traverse (staying roughly 6,400-6,600 ft) past the Buckner buttress, then follow a north-facing rock gully and permanent snowfield (7,000-7,200 ft) to the south-trending ridge west of Booker's summit. Finish up talus, slabs, and a short, somewhat exposed 3rd-class (locally 4th-class-step) gully/dike to the summit. Routefinding through Horseshoe Basin is the crux of the day, not the climbing itself.
overview: The standard route: hike the Cascade Pass/Sahale Arm trail, drop cross-country into Horseshoe Basin, traverse east below Mount Buckner, then climb the south-trending ridge/gully west of the summit to the top — a long Class 3 scramble with one short, exposed 3rd-class step.

current.approach: Drive the Cascade River Road (paved then gravel) 23.1 miles from Marblemount to the Cascade Pass Trailhead (~3,600 ft). Hike the Cascade Pass Trail 3.7 miles/1,700 ft gain to Cascade Pass (5,392 ft), then continue up the Sahale Arm Trail toward Sahale Glacier/Sahale Camp. Leave the maintained trail near Sahale Camp and descend cross-country into Horseshoe Basin as described above.
approach_variant_names: Horseshoe Basin at 6,400-6,600 ft to the north-facing gully and the permanent snowfield
current.descent: From the summit, retrace the south ridge/gully back down to the 7,000-7,200 ft snowfield, cross back over to the north-facing gully, and re-traverse Horseshoe Basin at 6,400-6,600 ft past the Buckner buttress to the snow-free gully below Sahale's south side (~6,600 ft). Climb back up to Sahale Arm/Sahale Camp and follow the maintained trail down through Cascade Pass to the trailhead. The Horseshoe Basin traverse is loose, slick in places, and easy to lose the correct line in both directions.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rack needed for the standard scramble; a short length of rope/webbing is optional for parties wanting a handline on the short 3rd/4th-class step below the summit.
current.pro_needs: Essentially a scramble; a rope and light rack are optional insurance for the short Class 3 sections and are not needed by parties comfortable soloing exposed talus and scree.

name: Borrowed Time
beta: Climbs steep, sometimes hollow-feeling ice (P1, WI5) into a corner of excellent ice (P2, WI4), a gully approach beneath a hanging dagger (P3, WI3), a technical M7/WI4 crux pitch through overhanging rock with thin gear (P4), a blue-ice traverse (P5, WI4), and a long steep snow/ice headwall (roughly 45-60 degrees with vertical ice steps) to the summit ridge.
overview: A serious 6-pitch WI5 M7 mixed and ice line up the central weakness of Sloan's west face, established in winter 2025 and finishing with a long steep snow/ice headwall to the summit ridge.

current.approach: Via the Bedal Creek Trailhead (FR 4096) to Sloan Peak's west face; boot directly up the central weakness of the west face to a flat basin below the first ice step.
approach_variant_names: Bedal Creek to the west face basin, then the central line beneath the dagger
current.descent: Descend via the Corkscrew Route, involving a couple of rappels and a lot of downclimbing, including sustained ~60-degree terrain and traversing. An alternative is a V-thread rappel descent down the nearby Superalpine line.
current.detailed_rack: 8-10 ice screws, a handful of knifeblades and beaks, at least one small angle piton, and a set of nuts; a double rack is recommended for optimal options.
current.pro_needs: Thin, technical mixed and ice protection — screws for the ice pitches, pitons (KBs/beaks/angle) for the M7 crux, where three fixed pitons are also present.

name: Southeast Face
beta: The standard approach ascends unroped via ledges on the east/southeast face to minimize rockfall danger. Parties typically establish camps at Boston Basin low camp (5,300 ft) or high camp (6,400 ft), then traverse via the Boston-Sahale saddle to access the summit route. Most ascents run roughly 10-11 hours from high camp to summit and back, per the detailed schedule. Rope is essential for descent via three rappel stations.
overview: Boston Peak has a fearsome reputation as one of the loosest summits in the North Cascades, and even its easiest line — the Southeast Face via the Quien Sabe Glacier — demands constant caution. First climbed in 1938 by Calder Bressler, Ray Clough, Bill Cox, and Tom Myers, the standard route gains the Sahale-Boston col from the Quien Sabe Glacier, crosses the head of the Boston Glacier past the bergschrund, then works up a series of ledges on the peak's east/southeast side to the airy summit. The climbing is not hard (Class 4, one roped pitch), but the rock quality makes it a serious undertaking where every hold must be tested.

current.approach: From the Boston Basin Trailhead, a pullout on Cascade River Road below the road end (~3,200 ft, roughly mile 21.7), follow the unmaintained but well-established boot path through forest and slide alder, climbing steeply into Boston Basin (~3.2 mi, ~3,100 ft gain). Most parties camp at the basin's high camp (~6,400 ft) to shorten summit day, though the low camp (~5,300 ft) is an option for slower groups. From high camp, an alpine start gets you roped up the Quien Sabe Glacier to the Sahale-Boston col (~8,200 ft), then across the head of the Boston Glacier past the bergschrund to the base of the southeast-side ledges. From there, ascend unroped via loose, sandy 3rd/4th-class ledges on the east/southeast face (to minimize rockfall exposure to parties below) to a crux move just below the summit ridge, then a short scramble to the top. Hazards: crevasse danger on the Quien Sabe/Boston Glacier crossing (worsens through the season as the bergschrund opens), loose rock on the face's ledges and crux, and typical North Cascades afternoon rockfall/softening — an alpine start is standard.
approach_variant_names: Quien Sabe Glacier to the Sahale-Boston col, then the connecting ridge
current.descent: Descend by reversing the approach to the summit ridge, then rappel rather than downclimb the loose upper face: from the summit, walk a few feet toward Sahale to the first rappel sling/station. Three rappels down the southeast/east face bring you back to the snow at the head of the Boston Glacier, near the base of the Sahale–Boston col. Multiple independent trip-report accounts describe the anchors as roughly 25m apart station-to-station but recommend carrying 60m ropes (used doubled, ~30m per pitch) so you are never left short between stations — bring extra webbing, since the fixed slings, while described as well-positioned and currently in good condition, are natural/gear anchors (slung horns and blocks, not bolts) and are exactly the kind of aging tat worth backing up before weighting. After the third rappel, reverse the glacier traverse back up to the Sahale–Boston col and descend the Quien Sabe Glacier to camp in Boston Basin, then the boot path back to the trailhead. Hazards on descent: rockfall in the rappel line (helmet on, and be mindful of parties above/below), softening snow bridges on the glacier walk-off in the afternoon, and the mountain's generally loose, exposed rock — Boston has a real fatality history and the descent should not be treated casually.
current.detailed_rack: Very light rack only: a small set of nuts and a handful of cams in the roughly 0.4-2in range for the short technical steps near the summit and to back up rappel anchors if needed. Full double racks are unnecessary — most of the route is unroped 4th-class scrambling on ledges, not sustained crack climbing. The three rappel stations along the standard descent (toward Sahale, then down) are described by parties as solid, pre-equipped anchors ('bomb proof'), so plan to supplement rather than build anchors from scratch; carry a few extra rap rings/cord/webbing in case a station needs backing up or refreshing.
current.pro_needs: Protection needs are minimal because most of the route is climbed unroped as 4th-class scrambling; the rock is notoriously loose and chossy with real rockfall danger, which is exactly why parties minimize roped/stacked climbing here. Where gear is placed (short steps, rappel backups) opportunities are limited and rock quality for protection is questionable — test everything. The three fixed rappel anchors on the standard descent are reported as solid, reducing the anchor-building burden.
current.rope_note: Descent is three ~25m single-strand rappels off fixed sling anchors on the way down toward Sahale/the snow below; a 60m rope doubled gives ~30m per strand, ample margin (even a 50m rope would work). Single rope is standard — nothing in trip reports supports carrying a second rope, and most of the route is climbed unroped anyway, further reducing rope-related weight concerns.

name: West Face of Boston
beta: The route begins below the west face and climbs steep snow heading NE for two pitches (belays under a bulge, then where a gully opens to the east), then follows a large gully east on pitch 3 (occasional rock hooks in the snow), continues up on pitch 4 to about 200 ft north of the summit, and finishes on pitch 5 across an exposed ridge to the true summit after a short rock step. A winter ascent found steep snow that grew icier and more rime-choked toward the north ridge, stayed on snow rather than take the harder mixed direct gully, and needed significant rime-ice removal to find gear and a bergschrund circumvented by climbing to climber's right.
overview: A 5-pitch, 650-ft steep snow-and-mixed line up Boston Peak's west face, first climbed in September 1956 and later given a documented first winter ascent; chosen by winter parties specifically to avoid the Southeast Face's lack of protection when icy.

current.approach: Winter approach: Cascade River Road to the Eldorado Trailhead gate, then bike/ski up Cascade Pass trail to the highest switchback, angle up to about 6,400 ft and drop into the Soldier Boy drainage, then rising-traverse to the Quien Sabe Glacier's NW corner and rope up for the glacier crossing. Summer access would follow the standard Boston Basin approach to the base of the west face.
approach_variant_names: The Quien Sabe's northwest corner to the lower of the two gullies
current.detailed_rack: A single rack of cams (small to #2) plus some nuts and pickets; on the first winter ascent, pitons and hexes proved more reliable than cams in icy cracks, and buried ski poles served as deadman anchors.
current.pro_needs: Mixed snow/ice/rock protection: cams and nuts for rock, pickets for snow, with pitons/hexes preferred over cams in icy or rimed cracks.

name: Boving Roofs
beta: Climb the first three pitches of the Southwest Rib, then go left at a ledge. A short, loose 5.2 pitch leads to a belay below the roofs; the money pitch pulls under and over double roofs at 5.10b with good gear, followed by an easy chimney into 5.9 thin hands to a ledge with great position, joining the upper Southwest Rib/South Arete descent.
overview: A well-regarded direct variation to the Southwest Rib, taking a striking double-roof ('money pitch') instead of the standard line before rejoining the Bear Hug pitch.

current.approach: Same start as the Southwest Rib: Blue Lake Trailhead, Blue Lake Trail ~1.25 miles to the NW clearing, climber's path up into the basin to the Y-shaped larch tree at the base of the Southwest Rib (left of the Southwest Couloir). Climb the first 3 pitches of the Southwest Rib (or approach via the Northwest Face/Boving-Pollock line), then go left at a ledge where the two roofs come into view — this is pitch 5 of the combined line, about 100 ft of sustained 5.10b climbing under and pulling through the double roofs. Watch for a loose block right at the start of the roof pitch.
approach_variant_names: Blue Lake Trail to the Y-shaped larch at the base of the Southwest Rib, then three pitches up before this route starts
current.descent: Do not reverse the roofs: rappelling back through an overhanging roof is awkward and not the documented practice. Climb the Southwest Rib's last two pitches (its 6th and 7th) to the true summit, then take the standard South Arete descent: downclimb the arete to the Rabbit Ears, then 3 single-rope rappels (60 m rope) from the bolted chain stations climber's right of the gully. They land at the foot of the South Arete, not at the Y-shaped larch where you started — walk back north across the foot of the Southwest Couloir for anything left there, then down the climbers' trail to the Blue Lake Trail. So the 3 rappels are the descent from the summit, not a way down from the roofs. If bailing below the roofs, natural gear anchors would be needed since no fixed rappel line down the roof pitch itself was documented.
current.detailed_rack: Rack for the Southwest Rib's initial pitches, plus doubles of 0.5-3" cams for the roofs.
rack: Cams 0.3–3in (single set, doubles in finger/hand sizes)
Doubles of 0.5–3in cams for the roof pitch
current.pro_needs: Roofs protect well with medium-to-large cams; watch for a loose block at the very start of the roof pitch.
current.rope_note: 3-pitch trad line on South Early Winters Spire's granite. Standard alpine rack to 3in, doubles of 0.5-3in cams for the roofs. This route's standard descent is via the South Arete (3 single-rope rappels on a 60m rope past the Rabbit Ears).

name: Bowling Alley (aka Regular Route)
beta: Ground-up bolted route established by Brenden Sullivan and Jim Yoder up a network of gullies on the southern flank; 4 pitches of easy-to-moderate climbing (5.2–5.6) on knobby, cobble-studded welded-tuff breccia, finishing through a band of basalt to a low-angle summit chute shared with Cobbles 101.
overview: The original, easiest way up Pinto Rock's South Face — a moderate 4-pitch line up a gully/groove system on the west side of the buttress, listed as the 'regular' route.

current.approach: From the NF-77 pullout, a well-used trail runs along the base of the formation. The West Face and North Side are different aspects of the same rock reached via short spurs off this main trail, generally under 15 minutes' walk from the parking pullout.
current.descent: From the top, move to the rappel anchor near a tree at the north end of the formation. With a single 60m rope, two rappels down bolted anchors return climbers to the base; with two ropes, one long rappel suffices. Tie stopper knots in the rope ends — the rappels can otherwise run the ends off the rock.
current.detailed_rack: 12 quickdraws total, mixing standard draws with a few longer alpine draws for the traversing P2 to reduce rope drag; no trad gear is used.
current.pro_needs: Fully bolted to chain/fixed anchors on every pitch — bring a standard set of 10–12 quickdraws plus a couple of alpine draws for the wandering gully/traverse sections. No trad rack required.
current.rope_note: Pinto Rock 'South Face' area, the published 'regular route.' 400ft/4 pitches, knobby welded-tuff rock; bolted throughout, with the option to sling an occasional knob.

name: South Ridge
beta: The usual way up comes from the west, which means a long way round even though the peak stands only about three miles from Trinity. From the Trinity Trailhead, the Buck Creek Trail (#1513) climbs about 9.6 miles and 3,100 ft to Buck Creek Pass. From the pass an unmaintained high route winds around the west side of Liberty Cap and south to High Pass; contour through the pass and under Mount Berge, climb a short Class 3 step onto the ridge just south of Point 7839, and walk down into Louis Creek Basin to camp. From the basin, broad pumice, talus and low-angle snow lead up the broad west shoulder toward the top, and loose, slabby schist with one short Class 3-4 step near a horn goes to the summit. Some parties come in over Little Giant Pass and the Napeequa valley instead. A direct line from King Lake on the east side exists but is brushy, involves a river ford, and is seldom used.
overview: Buck Mountain (8,534 ft) is the high point of the peaks ringing Buck Creek Pass in the Glacier Peak Wilderness, named for pioneer USFS surveyor Albert H. Sylvester. Its north and east faces are composed of dark, almost black schist that gives the summit a brooding look above the pass; the summit affords sweeping views of Glacier Peak (about 9 miles west), Clark Mountain (its taller parent peak, ~4 miles southwest), Liberty Cap, and Helmet Butte. First climbed in 1948 by Carl Suback and Ray Rigg, the peak is now one of the most popular scrambles in the area — typically climbed as a side trip from a multi-day backpack based at Buck Creek Pass, and rated as an Alpine Scramble.

current.approach: From the Trinity Trailhead (Glacier Peak Wilderness, self-issue wilderness permit at the kiosk) at the end of the Chiwawa River Road/FR-6200 (~2,800 ft), follow Buck Creek Trail #1513. The trail splits from the Chiwawa River Trail #1550 within the first mile and climbs steadily through forest; around mile 2.75-3 it crosses the upper Chiwawa River, where there is no longer a footbridge; look for a log crossing near the old bridge site and have a wading backup plan, since the river runs fast and deep in early season. Above the crossing the trail is a long, fairly shadeless, grinding ascent (mosquitoes/black flies are heavy in July) through forest and then subalpine meadow along the flank of Middle Ridge, opening into increasingly good wildflower and Glacier Peak views as you climb. At roughly 9.25-10 miles and about 3,000-3,300 ft of gain, the trail tops out at Buck Creek Pass (~5,800-5,900 ft) - one of the most scenic passes in the Cascades, with a reliable spring near the pass for water (last dependable source before the basin). Beyond the pass there is no maintained trail: pick up the well-used climbers'/boot path that switchbacks up toward Liberty Cap and the High Pass Trail junction, then leave that path to contour and traverse west/southwest, staying below Liberty Cap, into the upper basin below Buck Mountain's south and west aspects (Louis Creek Basin, ~6,700 ft) - the standard camp for a two-day trip. Follow the ridge crest through Class 2-3 terrain (stepping to locally 3-4 near a horn/gendarme close to the true summit) on loose, rubbly, slabby schist to the top; the summit crest has several bumps within feet of each other, so take care identifying the true high point. Primary approach hazards: rockfall/loose schist (helmet recommended, especially with parties above or below), the river crossing in high water, no reliable water source between the pass and the basin in a dry year, and route-finding above Buck Creek Pass since the climbers' path is intermittent. An alternate historic approach reaches Buck Mountain via Little Giant Pass and the Napeequa Valley, used for longer traverses.
approach_variant_names: Trinity to Buck Creek Pass, then the High Pass high route around the west side
Little Giant Pass and the Napeequa valley
current.descent: This is a walk-off/downclimb - no rappelling is involved on the standard South Ridge route. Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the Class 2-3 (locally 3-4 near the summit horn) loose, rubbly schist back down the ridge crest to the low-angle snowfield/basin around 7,400 ft, then descend the pumice and talus slopes back to the Louis Creek Basin camp (~6,700 ft). From there, traverse back east below Liberty Cap to rejoin the boot path down to Buck Creek Pass, and finish on the maintained Buck Creek Trail #1513 for the roughly 9.25-10 mile, ~3,000-3,300 ft descent back to the Trinity Trailhead. Trip reports on this route put summit-day round trip from a Buck Creek Pass/Louis Creek Basin camp at roughly 4 hours; given a car-to-car round trip of roughly 30 miles, most parties treat this as an overnight (camp at Buck Creek Pass or the upper basin) rather than a single push, though strong parties have done it in a long day. The main descent hazard is the same loose schist encountered on the way up - downclimbing loose rock is generally more dangerous than ascending it, so descend deliberately, test holds, and keep the group tight (or move one at a time) through the Class 3-4 band near the summit to avoid kicking rock onto climbers below. Rappels: 0.
current.detailed_rack: No roped rock rack is needed for the standard scramble line; it is climbed unroped in typical dry summer conditions. Some parties carry a light rope, a few slings, and basic protection for added security on the more exposed class 3 steps or if conditions are wet, icy, or snow-covered.
current.pro_needs: This is an unroped Class 2-3 scramble with no fixed protection or established rappel anchors; parties uncomfortable with the exposed schist moves near the summit sometimes carry a rope and a few slings for a hip-belay or short rappel, but it is not standard gear for this line.
bivy: Buck Creek Pass and the High Pass camps
current.rope_note: Exposed Class 3 scrambling that calls for gear and experience. A rope is not typically carried for the ridge scramble itself, as on comparable Class 3 Cascades scrambles, though some parties may carry a short rope/sling for exposed moves.

name: Southwest Slope via Marmot Pass
beta: From the Upper Big Quilcene Trailhead, Trail #833 climbs through old-growth forest past Shelter Rock Camp and Camp Mystery to the open alpine gap of Marmot Pass (~6,000 ft), one of the most scenic passes in the Olympics. From the pass, turn right onto the Tubal Cain Trail and follow it north about 100 m to a junction, then leave it and climb right up switchbacks along the ridge, over a minor ~6,800 ft knob, to Buckhorn's southwest summit (6,988 ft) — the higher of its two nearly-equal summits. The final approach is loose scree, not quite Class 3, finishing with a short scramble onto a large summit boulder. When snow-free, the route requires no technical gear or roped travel.
overview: Buckhorn Mountain is a double-summit peak in the Buckhorn Wilderness (Olympic National Forest), immediately outside the Olympic National Park boundary. The nearly-level west and east summits, about 1,200 ft apart across a smooth saddle, were thought to resemble deer antlers, giving the mountain its name. The standard route climbs the Upper Big Quilcene Trail over scenic 5,950 ft Marmot Pass, then leaves the trail for a short, rough scramble up the open southwest slope to the true (west) summit. It's widely used as an entry-level scramble/BCEP graduation objective — mostly Class 2 talus and boot path with one short Class 3 move onto the summit boulder, no rope required.

current.approach: From the Upper Big Quilcene Trailhead (~2,650 ft, end of FR-2750), the route follows the Upper Big Quilcene River Trail #833. The first 2.5 miles are an easy, mostly rolling grade through old-growth cedar and hemlock forest with the Big Quilcene River alongside you the whole way — this stretch is your last reliable, easy-access water for a while and there are no fords, just a trail paralleling the river. At about mile 2.5 you reach Shelter Rock Camp (~3,600 ft), a designated camp with water access. Past it, around mile 3.5, the trail pulls away from the river and climbs a sustained, steeper 3/4-mile pitch of switchbacks — the single steepest, most sustained grade on the approach — then continues climbing through subalpine forest and opens into meadows around mile 4.5 at Camp Mystery (~5,300 ft), the last camp and last dependable water source before the pass (treat before drinking). From Camp Mystery it's about another 0.5 mile of open meadow hiking to Marmot Pass (~6,000 ft) at mile 5, a major trail junction where the Tubal Cain Trail forks off toward Buckhorn Lake Camp/the old Tubal Cain Mine, and the main trail continues over the pass toward Home Lake and the Dungeness Trail. Buckhorn's summit route turns right (north) here onto the Tubal Cain Trail for only a short distance, then leaves it for the unsigned climbers'/boot path that climbs right up the open ridge crest roughly 1 mile and 900–1,000 ft of gain to the southwest (higher) summit. It's not an official trail — expect braided boot paths through heather and talus, a few spots where you'll want hands for balance, and a short, easy scramble onto the large boulder that forms the true high point. Route-finding is straightforward in clear weather (stay near the ridge crest) but the braided paths and cliffy drop-offs on the north side make it easy to wander off-line in fog or whiteout, so a GPS track or careful attention to the ridgeline is worthwhile. Lingering snow patches near Camp Mystery and the upper ridge are possible into early summer; a light axe/microspikes can help in that window, though by mid-summer the route is dry scree, talus, and heather.
approach_variant_names: Upper Big Quilcene Trail #833 over Marmot Pass
current.descent: Descend the same way you came up: reverse the boot path off the summit block, follow the ridge-crest climbers' trail back down to Marmot Pass (watch footing on the loose scree/talus sections — they're more tedious to downclimb than to ascend, and the braided paths can tempt you off-route, especially in poor visibility), then drop back onto the maintained Trail #833 through Camp Mystery, Shelter Rock Camp, and the forest to the trailhead. This is a standard walk-off/scramble descent — no technical downclimbing and no rappelling anywhere on the route. The only sustained knee-punishing stretch is the steep 3/4-mile switchback section between Shelter Rock Camp and Camp Mystery; otherwise it's a straightforward, well-graded trail hike back to the car.
current.pro_needs: None required -- this is a Class 2-3 scramble with no fixed protection.
bivy: Camp Mystery — the last water below Marmot Pass
Marmot Pass — high dry bivy on the crest
current.rope_note: From Marmot Pass, a steep open boot path gains the West Peak summit — an easy Class 2 scramble with one short Class 3 move onto the summit boulder, suitable as a first scramble, no technical gear needed.

name: Southwest Face / Southwest Slopes
beta: From Sahale Glacier Camp at 7,600 feet, descend the south ridge of Sahale Peak to Horseshoe Basin. Traverse across snowfields approximately 2 miles to the mountain's base. Ascend steep snowfields with the distinctive cow-skull-shaped snowfield as a navigational landmark. The climb involves navigating steepening snow chutes and slopes at 35-40 degrees. The final 100 feet is Class 2-3 rock scrambling to the summit block. Total route elevation gain from camp is approximately 3,000 feet.
overview: Buckner Mountain is the third-highest peak in North Cascades National Park, the 14th-highest summit in Washington, and 11th on the state's Bulger list of 100 highest peaks — one of only about ten non-volcanic Washington summits above 9,000 ft. The mountain has two summits of nearly equal height a short distance apart along the summit ridge; nearly all parties top out on the southwest (true) summit reached by this route. It crowns the ridge between Sahale Arm and Horseshoe Basin and is a coveted objective on multi-day Cascade Pass carryovers with Sahale and Boston Peak. The southwest side gives the standard non-technical line — long, but largely third- and fourth-class scrambling — most commonly reached from a high camp on Sahale Arm.

current.approach: Start from the Cascade Pass Trailhead (~3,600 ft) at the end of Cascade River Road/FR-15. Take the maintained Cascade Pass Trail, which switchbacks through old-growth forest and then traverses subalpine meadows to Cascade Pass (5,400 ft) at 3.7 mi / ~1,700 ft gain. From the pass, pick up the Sahale Arm Trail heading north/climber's-right: it climbs steadily through heather meadows, then over steepening rock and scree benches to the toe of the Sahale Glacier, ending at Sahale Glacier Camp (~7,600 ft) — 5.9 mi and ~3,940 ft gain one-way from the trailhead, and the standard high camp/base for the route (NPS permit and bear-canister required; camp only in the designated sites at the glacier's edge). Reliable water is available at camp from snowmelt/the glacier's edge early season; carry a stove or filter since Sahale Arm itself is dry above the meadows. From camp the route continues off-trail: descend Sahale Peak's south ridge on class 1-2 rock, then down a short class 3 step to a ~6,800 ft notch, and traverse roughly 2 miles across Horseshoe Basin (6,600-6,800 ft) on talus, slabs, and lingering snow, passing near the old Davenport Mine site (~7,000 ft) to reach the base of Buckner's southwest face. This basin traverse is exposed to rockfall and can require an axe/crampons for steep snow patches into midsummer — start early to avoid afternoon softening and thunderstorm exposure. From the base, climb steepening southwest-facing snowfields toward a distinctive 'cowskull-shaped' snowfield high on the face (the key navigational landmark, described by climbers as looking like a ghost early season); ascend a snow chute and then the cowskull itself, where the angle steepens enough that many parties place running-belay pickets. Above the snow, step off, remove crampons, and grovel up loose scree/rubble to the summit ridge, finishing with about 100 ft of class 2-3 rock scrambling to the true summit. Most parties take 2-3 days car-to-car given the ~20-mile round trip and 7,400 ft of gain, though strong parties have done it in one very long day.
approach_variant_names: Sahale Arm and Horseshoe Basin to the cowskull snowfield
current.descent: Descend the same southwest-slopes line used on ascent — this is a walk-off/downclimb route with no rappelling required (rappels: 0). From the summit, downclimb the scree/rubble and re-descend the cowskull snowfield and chute on the fall line to about 7,200 ft; steep snow here is typically managed by facing in and plunge-stepping or downclimbing with an ice-axe self-belay, and less experienced parties often protect it with a running belay on pickets. Continue down and traverse right to re-cross Horseshoe Basin on the broad ledge system at 6,200-6,400 ft (passing back near Davenport Mine), then ascend a short ~100 ft snow finger to regain the rounded ridge above the toe of Sahale's south ridge. From there, scramble back up the class 3 step and class 1-2 south ridge to Sahale Glacier Camp, and descend the Sahale Arm/Cascade Pass Trail 5.9 miles back to the Cascade Pass Trailhead. The main descent hazards are loose scree/rubble near the summit and sustained steep snow on the cowskull section (self-arrest skill required); no technical rope work is needed in normal summer conditions.
current.detailed_rack: No rock gear required; the line is a scramble.
current.pro_needs: None for the standard route.

name: South Ridge (Bullseye Traverse variant)
beta: From Bullseye Pass (~6,200 ft), parties drop packs and climb the steep southeast slope on foot/hands to grippy granite, working up and over a hump before dropping beneath the summit on its western side (Class 3 traverse). The final approach to the true summit follows the south ridge and requires roped Class 4-5.0 climbing — two independent accounts describe one to two short pitches on excellent, hold-covered granite, finishing with an exposed high step onto a one-person summit perch.
overview: A harder, more direct line up Bulls Tooth's south ridge from Bullseye Pass, done by parties on the multi-summit 'Bullseye Traverse'; unlike the standard notch scramble, this line finishes with a short, roped Class 4-5 pitch to the true summit.

current.approach: Reached via the Chain Lakes/Doelle Lakes basin as part of a multi-day traverse (e.g. the 'Bullseye Traverse'), continuing cross-country south to Bullseye Pass (~6,200 ft) before dropping packs and climbing the south side of the peak. No standalone trailhead-to-base mileage for this specific line is documented; it is climbed as a side trip from a traverse camp.
current.descent: From the summit, three rappels on a ~40m rope are needed to get back down through the technical section to easier ground; the granite here is compact with few holds and was reported as harder to reverse than to climb — one party found a heather-camouflaged hole in the rock during the down-climb. Below the rappels, reverse the Class 3 traverse back around the peak to Bullseye Pass.
current.pro_needs: A small rack of slings/runners was reported adequate by one party but inadequate by another attempting the northwest-ridge variant nearby — cams/small nuts add real protection given the sparse gear placements described.

name: North Face
beta: This is considered the standard and easiest route up Burgundy Spire. Descent is accomplished via 5 double-rope rappels down the middle of the upper face. Recommended for climbers experienced in alpine rock and comfortable with route-finding on exposed terrain. The route features many traverses, down-climbs, and loose features that demand careful attention.
overview: Burgundy Spire is the highest of the four Wine Spires (Burgundy, Chianti, Pernod, Chablis) on Silver Star Mountain's long north ridge above Washington Pass. Its North Face (5.8, Grade III) is the standard, most-climbed route up the peak — sustained, exposed alpine granite reached via a long, steep climber's trail to 7,770-ft Burgundy Col. Note: unlike Liberty Crack on nearby Liberty Bell, this route is not on Steck & Roper's 'Fifty Classic Climbs of North America' list — it is a well-regarded regional classic rather than a national one.

current.approach: From the SR-20 pullout (~4,310 ft, near milepost 166, about 3.75 mi east of Washington Pass and directly across the valley from Silver Star Mountain), a boot path drops down through loose talus to the east into forest — this is the trailhead for the shared Burgundy Col approach (there's no numbered Forest Service trail; it's an established but unofficial boot path). A short way in, pass a wilderness trail-register box, then ford Early Winters Creek on logs at about 4,080 ft (can run swift and cold in early season). From the creek, the path climbs steadily east through forest and then open slopes, gaining roughly 2,200 ft to a broad, flat bench at ~6,460 ft that fits a dozen-plus tents and is the natural approach midpoint and best high camp. Beyond the bench, the trail climbs and traverses loose scree gullies below Burgundy's northwest aspect before a final, cairn-marked stretch of notoriously unstable 'ball-bearing' scree over slab (careful class 2, worse on the way down) up to Burgundy Col at roughly 7,770–7,800 ft, the narrow notch between Burgundy Spire and Paisano Pinnacle. Total is about 3 miles and 3,500–4,000 ft of gain one-way to the col, with the North Face route starting essentially right above it — the route and first pitch are visually obvious once you're at the col. Water sources: Early Winters Creek near the start, a small trickle on the trail below the col, and occasionally a patch of hard snow/ice on the col's east side late-season. The main approach hazards are the creek ford in early season and the loose scree below the col, which is prone to kicking rockfall onto climbers below — travel tightly grouped and be deliberate with foot placement on that final pitch.
approach_variant_names: Burgundy Col in a single push
Camp at the 6,460 ft bench
current.descent: From the summit, the descent is 5 double-rope rappels down the face back to Burgundy Col, then a reversal of the approach. Specifically: R1 (~40m) from a large, heavily slung boulder at the summit down the middle of the upper face to a bolted anchor on a ledge; R2 (~55m) from the bolts down lichen-covered rock to a huge ledge near a rock arch — traverse the ledge to a constriction where slings back up the next anchor; R3 (~55m) from that constriction down more lichen-covered rock to a horn with a blue sling (climber's right of the ascent line); R4 (~40m) from that horn down to broad, scree-covered upper ledges — pull the rope carefully here, as there's real potential to snag it on the ledge system; R5 (~60m) down over the lower scramble terrain, landing back at Burgundy Col where the route starts. Double 60m ropes are the standard setup; parties have gotten down with a single 60–70m rope and some added downclimbing between stances (more, shorter rappels than the five double-rope ones; one party logged 9-10), but that's tighter and involves more exposed downclimbing on loose terrain. Anchors are a mix of slung natural features (boulder, horn) and fixed bolts/webbing — inspect webbing before weighting it, since it's exposed to UV and can be old. Once at the base of the last rappel, reverse the Burgundy Col approach (down the loose scree, then the boot path past the flat bench and creek crossing) back to the highway pullout.
current.detailed_rack: 60m rope x2 (doubles strongly preferred for the 5-rappel descent — single-rope parties need an intermediate anchor at the big ledge); full nut set; cams to 4 inches (a #4-equivalent placed a few times on route); about 10 alpine draws. Consider doubling 0.5–1 in cams if 5.8 is near your limit.
current.pro_needs: Solid alpine rock pro across the grade; some natural placements.

current.rope_note: Standard practice is two 60m ropes carried together (one used for leading, both joined for double-rope rappels). The 5-rappel descent is staged for double-rope lengths (~40/55/55/40/60m per a firsthand account). Another trip report confirms a single 60m rope is a viable fallback (minor downclimbing required) and a single 70m eliminates that issue, but doubles remain the majority-recommended approach across all sources reviewed.

name: North Route
beta: This is the peak's standard (easiest) route, reached from the Dutch Miller Gap Trail. After a long approach and a cold river ford, parties climb through brush and talus on the peak's north side to about 5,400 ft, then ascend a gully (reported as a northeast gully) that holds a steep snow ramp and a moat into mid-summer, before boulder-hopping the final talus to the summit. It is described as seldom visited, with real route-finding and bushwhacking involved; a neighboring northwest gully is reported to involve Class 4 terrain and should be avoided.
overview: Burnt Boot Peak (6,540 ft) is a remote, lightly-visited summit in the western Alpine Lakes Wilderness, about 6.5 miles northeast of Snoqualmie Pass in eastern King County. It sits near the head of Burnboot Creek, roughly 1.3 miles from Lemah Mountain, and is reached from the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River drainage (Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest) rather than the more heavily traveled Salmon La Sac/PCT side of the wilderness. The standard north-side route is a trailless scramble — a river ford, talus, a brushy gully, and a short steep snow pitch below the summit pass — that sees only a handful of ascents most years.

current.approach: Park at the Dingford Creek Trailhead, where Middle Fork Snoqualmie Road (FS Road 56) is gated to vehicles — the last few miles of FS 56 are pitted with potholes and washboard, so high-clearance is strongly recommended — then walk or bike about 7.5 mi of closed road to its old end at the former Dutch Miller Gap Trailhead (Trail #1030). Do not follow the maintained Dutch Miller Gap trail; instead ford the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River roughly 300 ft upstream of the trailhead to its true-right (north) bank. Early-season and post-snowmelt (roughly June) this ford can run thigh-deep and cold — scout upstream for a braided or log crossing if flows are high. Once across, climb the boulder/talus field directly above the river for about 400 vertical feet until you hit a rock band. At the cliff, angle left (west) into a brushy gully thick with salmonberry and black currant — expect real bushwhacking here, not a trail. Follow the gully up into timber around 3,900 ft, then traverse upward through the trees until you break out onto open talus. From the talus, work up and climber's-left toward the low notch/pass beside Point 5,841, which separates Burnt Boot's summit block from the peak immediately west — this notch is the key route-finding target and where the described 'heather/cedar benches' sit. Above roughly 5,400–5,800 ft, pick a line through talus and boulders to avoid the steepest snow; the final ~200 vertical feet below the pass typically holds a firm, sustained snow ramp well into summer, and an ice axe (crampons/microspikes in early season) is required for this section — it is genuine self-arrest terrain. From the pass, a short class 3–4 ridge traverse leads to the summit. From the ford the summit is roughly 2 mi one way, with nearly all the elevation gain packed into the final two miles above the river. There is no reliable water once you leave the river, aside from occasional early-season snowmelt trickles near the pass. Principal hazards: the river ford itself, sustained brush in the lower gully, loose talus/scree on the upper slopes, and the steep snow ramp below the pass. Near the top of the summit-pass snow ramp, watch for a moat-type gap — a short traverse beneath the snow edge may be needed to reach solid rock.
approach_variant_names: Middle Fork ford and the north-side gully
current.descent: Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the short class 3–4 ridge step off the summit block back to the Point 5,841 pass, then descend the steep snow ramp below it facing in, plunge-stepping or self-belaying with an ice axe (a controlled glissade may be possible lower down if the snow is soft and the runout is clean and known — check before committing). From the base of the ramp, work back down through talus and boulders, staying climber's-right where possible to avoid the loosest scree, drop into the timber, and downclimb the brushy salmonberry/currant gully back to the cliff band. Pick a descending line through the boulder field to the river and re-ford to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb — there is no fixed rappel station or bolted anchor on this route, and the discipline (scrambling, not roped climbing) is consistent with that. In icy or wet conditions some parties might choose to build a single natural rappel (sling around a horn or tree) to protect the short class 4 step just above the pass, but that is a judgment call, not standard practice for the route. Note there is a separate, much harder roped North Ridge line on this peak (1971 first ascent by Williamson/Oas/Bucher, three leads of 5th-class granite) that is a distinct technical route from this scramble line and should not be confused with it.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is needed on the standard Class 3 line; it is a scramble, not a roped climb.
current.pro_needs: No fixed or removable rock protection is typically placed on the standard route. Carry an ice axe and helmet for the snow gully and loose rock; a short section of steep snow/moat may warrant extra caution or a rope for less experienced parties in early season.
bivy: Hardscrabble Horse Camp, Middle Fork Snoqualmie
current.rope_note: Class 3 scramble on solid granite (per the North Ridge first-ascent account: 3 leads class 3-4 above a class 5 base section). No rope needed for the standard scramble line; parties climbing the true north ridge crest into 5th class terrain should carry a short rope.
